questions.title: Isolation Levels and Concurrency Control as an Organization-Wide Platform Decision
questions.prompt: You're setting a default transaction isolation policy for every OLTP-adjacent service feeding your data platform -- dozens of teams, mixed SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake-backed services. Some teams want strict serializability for correctness; others want maximum throughput. Walk through how you'd reason about isolation-level tradeoffs at this scale, and what default you'd mandate versus what you'd let teams override.
questions.modelAnswer: At platform scale, isolation level stops being a per-query tuning knob and becomes a policy decision with real organizational cost on both sides: too strict and you manufacture contention and deadlocks across dozens of independently-deployed services sharing resources; too loose and you create classes of correctness bugs (phantom reads, write skew) that only show up under real concurrent load, long after the team that wrote the query has moved on. My default mandate would be read-committed snapshot isolation (or Postgres's default MVCC-backed read committed) everywhere, because it eliminates the vast majority of reader/writer blocking without requiring every team to reason about anomalies, at the acceptable cost of tempdb/version-store overhead that's cheap compared to engineer-hours spent debugging deadlocks. I'd carve out an explicit exception process for serializable or SNAPSHOT isolation for specific, documented invariants -- financial ledger balance checks, inventory reservation logic -- where write skew is a real correctness risk, requiring the team to demonstrate they've scoped the serializable transaction as narrowly as possible. I would not let teams default to READ UNCOMMITTED/NOLOCK platform-wide; that's an anti-pattern I'd only approve for a specific, reviewed reporting query, never as a blanket setting. The governance mechanism matters as much as the default: a lightweight architecture review for any team requesting an exception, documented in one place, so the next engineer understands why a given service's isolation level differs from the norm instead of discovering it as a surprise during an incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set one default for the whole platform and build a narrow, documented exception path rather than let each team pick for themselves, because inconsistent isolation levels across dozens of services is exactly the kind of thing that turns into a three-day incident investigation nobody can explain. My default is read-committed snapshot isolation or its Postgres equivalent -- it kills most of the lock contention teams actually complain about, with no code changes, and the tempdb cost is trivial next to the engineering time saved. For the handful of services doing something like balance reservation or inventory holds where write skew is a real risk, I'd ask them to bring me the specific invariant they're protecting and we'd scope a serializable transaction narrowly around just that operation, not the whole service. What I won't sign off on is NOLOCK as a platform default -- I've seen it get reached for as a quick fix for blocking and then quietly cause data correctness bugs that take months to surface. I'd rather spend a week reviewing three exception requests than debug a silent correctness bug in a ledger six months from now.
commonMistakes: Treats isolation level as a per-team preference instead of a platform-wide policy decision
Defaults to the loosest isolation level to maximize throughput without weighing correctness risk
Allows NOLOCK/READ UNCOMMITTED as a blanket default rather than a narrowly reviewed exception
No governance process for exceptions, leading to undocumented divergence across services
Ignores that the decision spans multiple SQL dialects with different default behaviors (SQL Server vs PostgreSQL vs Snowflake)
keyPoints: Frames isolation level as an org-wide policy decision, not a per-query tuning choice
Recommends read-committed snapshot / MVCC as the sane default at scale
Reserves serializable/snapshot isolation for specific, documented correctness invariants
Explicitly rejects NOLOCK as a platform default
Builds a lightweight, documented exception/review process rather than ad hoc divergence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about isolation-level tradeoffs at organizational scale
Chooses a defensible default and justifies it
Defines a clear, bounded exception path rather than unlimited team autonomy
Rejects unsafe shortcuts (NOLOCK) as a general policy

questions.title: Migrating a Legacy SQL Estate: Why Data Types Are the Easy Part
questions.prompt: Your organization is migrating 400+ stored procedures from a legacy SQL Server estate to a target cloud warehouse dialect. Leadership believes this is mostly a data-type mapping exercise. Explain why that's wrong, what actually consumes most of the effort in a migration like this, and how you'd sequence and de-risk the work.
questions.modelAnswer: Data type mapping -- DATETIME to TIMESTAMP, MONEY to NUMERIC, and so on -- is mechanical and largely automatable; it's genuinely the easy 20% of the work. The expensive 80% is procedural logic: cursors, nested transactions with custom error handling, recursive CTEs with platform-specific quirks, temp table scoping rules, IDENTITY/sequence semantics, and especially implicit behaviors like T-SQL's SET-based error handling versus a target dialect's exception model, which don't translate line-for-line and instead require re-architecting the procedure's control flow. Equally expensive is the testing burden: with 400+ procedures, you cannot manually verify correctness one-by-one, so the migration has to produce a before/after result-set diff harness run against representative production-shaped data for every procedure, or you will ship silent logic regressions that surface as wrong numbers in a report three months later. I'd sequence this by first cataloging and scoring every procedure by complexity (cursor-free, set-based logic first; procedural, stateful logic last) and by business criticality, then migrate the low-risk tier first to validate the tooling and diff harness, then tackle the complex tier in small batches with a mandatory shadow-run period where both the old and new implementations run in parallel and are diffed before the new one is trusted. I would never accept 'it looks like the same logic' as a migration sign-off criterion.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct that assumption early and gently, because if leadership thinks this is a type-mapping exercise, the timeline they've set is going to be wrong by a wide margin. The types really are the easy part -- that's a few hours with a mapping table. What eats months is the procedural logic: cursors that don't have a clean equivalent, error handling that behaves completely differently across dialects, and a hundred small implicit assumptions baked into procedures written over a decade by different people. My pitch to leadership is always the same: we're not migrating syntax, we're re-verifying business logic, and the only way to do that safely at 400 procedures is a diff harness that runs the old and new versions side by side against real data shapes and flags any mismatch, because nobody can eyeball 400 procedures and be confident. I sequence the simple, stateless ones first to prove the harness works, then work through the gnarly stateful ones in small batches with a shadow-run period, and I don't let anyone call a procedure 'migrated' until its diff has actually run clean, not just compiled clean.
commonMistakes: Treats data-type mapping as the dominant cost of the migration
Underestimates procedural-logic re-architecture (cursors, error handling, transaction scoping)
Has no automated before/after diff harness, relying on manual review at scale
Sequences migration by file order rather than by complexity and business criticality
Declares success based on successful compilation rather than verified behavioral equivalence
keyPoints: Identifies data-type mapping as mechanical and low-cost compared to procedural logic
Names specific procedural-logic risks: cursors, error handling, transaction scoping, implicit platform behavior
Proposes an automated result-set diff harness as the real correctness gate
Sequences migration by complexity and business risk, not arbitrary order
Defines 'migrated' as behaviorally verified, not merely syntactically translated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies procedural logic, not type mapping, as the dominant cost
Proposes a concrete verification/diff strategy at scale
Defines a sensible, risk-aware sequencing strategy
Sets a rigorous, behavior-based definition of migration success

questions.title: Lambda vs. Kappa at Platform Scale
questions.prompt: A VP asks you to justify, in plain terms, why your platform runs both a batch and a streaming path for some domains (Lambda) but a single streaming-first path for others (Kappa). Explain the real tradeoffs between the two architectures at large scale, and the criteria you use to decide which one fits a given domain.
questions.modelAnswer: Lambda architecture runs separate batch and streaming paths against the same raw data, reconciling them into a serving layer; its core value is that the batch path acts as a durable, replayable source of truth that can recompute correct results from scratch, which matters enormously when your stream-processing logic has a bug or your business logic changes retroactively, at the real cost of maintaining two codebases that must produce consistent results. Kappa collapses this into a single streaming path, treating the event log itself (e.g., Kafka with long or infinite retention) as the source of truth that can be replayed through the same streaming logic to reprocess history, which removes the dual-codebase maintenance burden but requires your streaming engine and storage to genuinely support cheap, complete reprocessing at the retention window you need -- not a given at petabyte scale, where reprocessing years of history through a stream processor is often slower and more expensive than a batch recompute over columnar storage. My criterion: if a domain has complex, evolving business logic that changes materially over its lifetime (fraud rules, pricing logic) and correctness-on-reprocess matters more than architectural simplicity, I lean Lambda, accepting the dual-path cost. If a domain's logic is comparatively stable and the data volume/replay cost favors a single pipeline (metrics, clickstream enrichment), I lean Kappa. The honest answer to the VP is that this isn't inconsistency -- it's matching the architecture to each domain's actual reprocessing and correctness needs rather than picking one orthodoxy platform-wide.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the VP directly: having both isn't an accident or technical debt, it's a deliberate decision because the two domains have genuinely different needs. For fraud detection, our rules change constantly and when they do, we need to be able to recompute history correctly -- that's exactly what the batch path in a Lambda setup gives us, a trustworthy from-scratch recompute whenever the streaming logic or the rules themselves change. Maintaining two codebases for that domain is a real cost, and I don't pretend otherwise, but it's cheaper than the alternative: discovering six months later that a streaming-only reprocess of two years of fraud events is either prohibitively slow or, worse, subtly wrong. For clickstream enrichment, the logic barely changes and the volume makes a single Kappa-style streaming path with a well-retained Kafka log the simpler, cheaper choice -- there's no serious reprocessing risk to hedge against. So the rule I apply is: how often does this domain's logic change, and how expensive and risky is a full reprocess if it does? That answer tells you which architecture actually fits, and forcing one pattern everywhere would just be trading real architectural fit for false consistency.
commonMistakes: Treats Lambda and Kappa as a universal either/or choice rather than a per-domain fit decision
Ignores the dual-codebase consistency burden Lambda imposes
Assumes Kappa's replay capability is free regardless of retention volume and reprocessing cost
Can't articulate concrete criteria for choosing between them
Presents running both as inconsistency rather than a deliberate, justified decision
keyPoints: Explains Lambda's batch-path value: durable, replayable, correctness-on-reprocess
Explains Kappa's tradeoff: simpler single path, but depends on cheap full replay at scale
Names the dual-codebase consistency cost of Lambda honestly
Gives a concrete decision criterion (logic volatility + reprocessing cost/risk)
Frames running both patterns across domains as deliberate fit, not inconsistency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains both architectures' mechanics and tradeoffs
Provides a concrete, defensible decision criterion
Honestly addresses the costs of each approach
Communicates the reasoning clearly to a non-technical executive

questions.title: Applying CAP Theorem to a Real Multi-Region Platform Decision
questions.prompt: Your platform is expanding to a second region for disaster recovery and latency reasons. A junior architect proposes a multi-region data store that's 'always consistent and always available, with no tradeoffs.' Use the CAP theorem to explain why that's not possible under a network partition, and walk through the actual consistency-vs-availability choice you'd make for (a) the metadata catalog and (b) the event ingestion layer.
questions.modelAnswer: CAP theorem states that under a network Partition -- which is a question of when, not if, across regions -- a distributed system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a response), it cannot guarantee both simultaneously; you can always have both in the common case when the network is healthy, which is exactly what makes 'no tradeoffs' sound plausible until the partition actually happens. For the metadata catalog -- table definitions, access grants, schema versions -- I'd choose consistency (CP) over availability during a partition: serving a stale or conflicting schema/grant to a query engine risks silent correctness or security violations, which is worse than a short availability gap while the partition resolves, so I'd accept that catalog writes may be rejected or delayed cross-region during a split rather than risk divergent metadata. For the event ingestion layer, I'd choose availability (AP): dropping or rejecting incoming events during a partition is usually worse than accepting writes locally in each region and reconciling/deduplicating them once connectivity is restored, because event data is typically append-only and idempotent-reconcilable, while metadata conflicts are not. The honest answer to the junior architect: there's no setting that avoids this choice, there's only choosing which failure mode (stale/rejected reads vs. temporarily unavailable writes) is less damaging for each specific subsystem, and that choice differs by subsystem within the same platform.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use this as a teaching moment rather than just shutting the idea down, because the instinct is understandable -- it would be great if we didn't have to choose. But a network partition between regions is a when, not an if, and the CAP theorem is really just naming what happens at that moment: you can keep answering requests, or you can guarantee every answer is the latest truth, and during the actual partition you cannot do both. So I'd walk through two concrete pieces of our platform where the right answer is genuinely different. The catalog -- schemas, grants -- I want consistent even if that means some operations get rejected during a split, because serving someone a stale permission grant is a security incident waiting to happen, not just an inconvenience. Event ingestion is the opposite: if a region goes dark for ten minutes, I'd much rather keep accepting events locally and reconcile duplicates afterward than tell every producer in that region 'sorry, try again later' -- a dropped or delayed event is recoverable, a security-relevant stale read is not. I'd tell the junior architect: the goal isn't finding the system with no tradeoff, it's matching the tradeoff to what's actually at stake in each part of the platform.
commonMistakes: Claims a system can be both perfectly consistent and perfectly available during an actual partition
Applies the same CP or AP choice uniformly to every subsystem instead of reasoning per-subsystem
Confuses CAP theorem's partition-specific tradeoff with general-purpose availability/latency tuning
Doesn't connect the choice to concrete failure-mode consequences (stale grants vs. dropped events)
Treats the question as purely theoretical rather than a real architecture decision with consequences
keyPoints: Correctly states CAP's actual claim: the tradeoff applies specifically during a network partition
Rejects the premise of a tradeoff-free multi-region system
Chooses CP for the metadata catalog with a concrete justification
Chooses AP for event ingestion with a concrete justification
Recognizes the CP/AP choice can and should differ by subsystem within one platform

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly and precisely explains CAP theorem's actual claim
Makes and justifies a CP choice for the metadata catalog
Makes and justifies an AP choice for event ingestion
Articulates that the CP/AP choice is subsystem-specific, not platform-wide

questions.title: Unity Catalog Metastore Topology for a Multi-Workspace, Multi-Region Org
questions.prompt: Your company runs 30+ Databricks workspaces across three Azure/AWS regions, grown largely by acquisition, with inconsistent governance. As the platform architect, explain how Unity Catalog's metastore-to-workspace topology actually works, and what metastore/catalog structure you'd standardize on to get consistent governance without forcing every workspace into one region.
questions.modelAnswer: A Unity Catalog metastore is a regional, account-level construct -- one metastore per region, and every workspace in that region can be (and typically should be) attached to the same regional metastore, which is what gives you one consistent governance surface (grants, lineage, audit logs, Delta Sharing) across all workspaces in that region rather than per-workspace Hive metastores with no shared story. Given 30+ workspaces across three regions grown by acquisition, the realistic target state is one metastore per region (not one globally, since metastores don't span regions) with a standardized catalog structure underneath each: typically an environment-oriented top level (catalogs for prod/staging/dev, or for business-unit-plus-environment if units have divergent compliance needs), with schemas underneath mapping to domains or source systems. I would not let each acquired business unit keep its own siloed metastore-equivalent governance model; the migration plan is to attach every workspace in a region to that region's single metastore, then systematically re-home existing managed/external tables and re-issue grants against the new catalog structure in batches, business-unit by business-unit, verifying lineage and access continuity at each step rather than a big-bang cutover. Cross-region access needs its own answer -- Delta Sharing or cross-region catalog federation for the specific tables that genuinely need to be read across regions -- rather than trying to force one metastore to serve multiple regions, which Unity Catalog doesn't support.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd correct is the mental model: people sometimes assume Unity Catalog is one global thing, but a metastore is actually scoped per region, so the real target isn't 'one metastore for the company,' it's 'one metastore per region, and every workspace in that region attaches to it.' With 30-plus workspaces grown by acquisition, I'd bet each acquired team brought its own ad hoc governance habits, so step one is just getting every workspace in a given region onto that region's single metastore -- that alone is what unlocks consistent grants, lineage, and audit logs instead of 30 different stories. Underneath that, I'd standardize catalogs around environment first, then business unit or domain where compliance actually requires separation, so we're not inventing a bespoke structure for every acquired team. I wouldn't try to do this as one big cutover -- I'd migrate business unit by business unit, re-homing tables and re-issuing grants, checking lineage didn't break at each step, because a big-bang Unity Catalog migration across that many workspaces is exactly the kind of thing that creates a governance incident, not fixes one. For the genuinely cross-region use cases, I'd reach for Delta Sharing rather than pretending one metastore can straddle regions, because it can't.
commonMistakes: Assumes a single Unity Catalog metastore can span multiple regions
Proposes keeping each acquired business unit's own siloed governance model instead of consolidating
Attempts a big-bang cross-org cutover instead of a staged, business-unit-by-business-unit migration
No plan for cross-region data access (Delta Sharing / federation)
Conflates workspace count with metastore count
keyPoints: Correctly states metastores are regional, one per region, shared across workspaces in that region
Proposes a standardized catalog structure (environment and/or business-unit/domain)
Plans a staged, verifiable migration rather than a big-bang cutover
Addresses cross-region access via Delta Sharing/federation rather than forcing a single metastore
Recognizes acquisition-driven governance drift as the real problem to fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Unity Catalog's regional metastore topology
Proposes a sound, standardized catalog/schema structure
Designs a realistic, staged migration plan for 30+ workspaces
Addresses cross-region data access correctly

questions.title: Fabric Capacity Model: Why 'Just Add a Bigger SKU' Isn't a Governance Strategy
questions.prompt: A Fabric capacity (F64) is being shared by six business units' workspaces, and whenever one team runs a heavy Spark job, everyone else's reports slow down or throttle. Leadership's instinct is to buy a bigger capacity SKU. Explain how Fabric capacity actually allocates compute across workspaces, why a bigger SKU alone doesn't solve the underlying governance problem, and what you'd actually implement.
questions.modelAnswer: Fabric capacity is a shared, finite pool of compute units (CUs) that every workspace assigned to that capacity draws from concurrently; it uses a smoothing/bursting model where short spikes borrow against future capacity, but sustained heavy usage from one workspace (a large Spark job, a heavy Direct Lake refresh) consumes CUs that every other workspace on the same capacity needs, which is exactly the noisy-neighbor symptom described. Buying a bigger SKU raises the ceiling and buys time, but it doesn't fix the governance gap: without workspace-level usage visibility and limits, the heaviest team will simply grow to consume whatever headroom you give them, and you'll be back in the same conversation at the next SKU tier, now paying considerably more. What I'd actually implement: first, use the Fabric Capacity Metrics app to get per-workspace CU consumption visibility so the conversation moves from 'everything is slow' to 'this specific workspace's job consumed this much, at this time' -- most noisy-neighbor disputes resolve immediately once there's a number attached to blame. Second, segment business units with genuinely heavy, unpredictable workloads (ad hoc Spark/ML) onto their own capacity, separate from units running predictable BI/reporting workloads, so a single team's spike can't starve six others' dashboards. Third, set workload-level guardrails (scheduling heavy jobs during low-usage windows, Spark pool sizing limits) rather than relying purely on capacity size. A bigger SKU may still be part of the answer, but only after the usage data shows it's genuinely needed, not as the first and only lever.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'buy a bigger SKU' as the first move, because without knowing what's actually driving the usage, we'd just be buying ourselves a few more months before we're back in this exact conversation at a higher price point. Fabric capacity is a shared pool across every workspace assigned to it, so when one business unit runs something heavy, everyone else genuinely does feel it -- that's not a bug, that's how the smoothing and shared-capacity model works. The first thing I'd actually do is turn on the Capacity Metrics app and get real per-workspace numbers, because right now this is 'everything feels slow' with no owner, and nine times out of ten once you can point at a workspace and a time window, the conversation changes completely. From there, I'd separate the business units with heavy, bursty Spark or ML workloads onto their own capacity, away from the teams just running steady reporting -- that's the actual fix for the noisy-neighbor problem, not a bigger shared pool that just raises everyone's blast radius together. If the data genuinely shows we need more total compute after that segmentation, I'm fine recommending a bigger SKU -- but as the second move, backed by numbers, not the reflexive first one.
commonMistakes: Treats a bigger capacity SKU as a complete fix rather than a temporary ceiling raise
Has no per-workspace usage visibility before recommending a solution
Doesn't consider segmenting heavy/bursty workloads onto separate capacities
Ignores Fabric's smoothing/bursting consumption model when diagnosing the symptom
Proposes a fix with no measurement or verification step
keyPoints: Explains Fabric's shared capacity/CU consumption and smoothing/bursting model
Identifies that a bigger SKU doesn't address the underlying governance gap
Proposes per-workspace usage visibility via the Capacity Metrics app
Recommends segmenting heavy/unpredictable workloads onto separate capacities
Treats a larger SKU as a data-justified option, not the default first move

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Fabric's shared capacity consumption model
Correctly identifies why a bigger SKU alone is insufficient
Proposes concrete visibility and segmentation measures
Treats the SKU upgrade as a justified, data-driven option rather than the default

questions.title: Snowflake Multi-Cluster Warehouses and Resource Monitors as Cost Governance
questions.prompt: Explain, at a mechanical level, how Snowflake multi-cluster warehouses scale concurrency versus how warehouse size scales per-query performance, and how you'd design resource monitors as an actual cost-governance control for a platform with 40+ teams self-serving their own warehouses.
questions.modelAnswer: These solve two different problems and conflating them is the most common Snowflake cost mistake at scale. Warehouse size (XS through 6X-Large) scales vertical compute for a single query -- more nodes available to parallelize one query's work -- and is the right lever when individual queries are slow due to genuine data volume or complexity. Multi-cluster warehouses scale horizontal concurrency: when query queuing occurs because too many concurrent queries are competing for one warehouse's compute, Snowflake can spin up additional clusters of the same size (auto-scale between a configured min and max) to serve more queries in parallel, then scale back down -- it does not make any individual query faster. The common expensive mistake is upsizing a warehouse to fix queuing (which doesn't help, since the queue was a concurrency problem, not a per-query speed problem) or adding more clusters to fix a single slow query (which doesn't help either, since one query still only runs on one cluster). For governance across 40+ self-serving teams, resource monitors are the actual control: I'd set a credit quota per warehouse or warehouse group tied to each team's budget, with graduated actions -- notify at 50-75%, suspend new queries at 100% -- rather than a single hard cutoff that silently breaks a team's pipeline mid-run with no warning. I'd pair that with mandatory auto-suspend (60-300 seconds of idle) on every warehouse so nobody pays for idle compute by default, and a required tagging/query-tag convention so spend is attributable to a team and workload, not just a warehouse name, which is what actually makes a resource-monitor alert actionable instead of just alarming.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd clear up first, because I see this mistake constantly, is that warehouse size and multi-cluster are not two versions of the same lever -- they fix two different symptoms. If one query is genuinely slow because it's chewing through real data volume, making the warehouse bigger helps. If queries are fast individually but piling up in a queue because fifteen people hit the same warehouse at once, making it bigger does nothing -- that's a concurrency problem, and multi-cluster is the actual fix, because it adds more clusters to serve requests in parallel rather than making any one of them faster. Once teams understand that distinction, half of the unnecessary cost disappears on its own. For the governance side, with 40-plus teams self-serving warehouses, I don't rely on people remembering to be careful -- I set a resource monitor with a real credit quota per warehouse, tied to what that team's actually budgeted for, with a notification at around three-quarters of quota and a suspend at full quota, so nobody wakes up to a surprise bill or, just as bad, has their pipeline silently killed with zero warning. And every warehouse gets auto-suspend after a short idle window as a non-negotiable default, because idle compute sitting around because nobody set that is pure waste that adds up fast across 40 teams.
commonMistakes: Upsizes a warehouse to fix query queuing instead of adding multi-cluster concurrency
Adds multi-cluster scaling to fix one slow individual query
Sets a single hard resource-monitor cutoff with no graduated warning before suspension
Doesn't enforce auto-suspend as a default, leaving idle compute running
No tagging/attribution convention, making cost alerts non-actionable at 40+ teams
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes warehouse size (per-query speed) from multi-cluster (concurrency)
Identifies the common mistake of conflating the two levers
Designs resource monitors with graduated notify/suspend thresholds
Mandates auto-suspend as a cost-governance default
Requires tagging/attribution so alerts map to an owning team and workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes warehouse size from multi-cluster scaling
Designs a real resource-monitor cost-governance strategy
Proposes auto-suspend and attribution as concrete controls
Addresses the scale (40+ self-serving teams) specifically

questions.title: Exactly-Once Semantics Across a Chain of Independently-Owned Systems
questions.prompt: Your event pipeline chains Kafka producers, a stream processor, and two downstream consumers owned by different teams, each writing to a different sink. Explain why 'exactly-once' is much harder to guarantee across this whole chain than within any single hop, and what you'd actually require of each team to get as close to exactly-once effective outcomes as realistically possible.
questions.modelAnswer: Kafka's own exactly-once semantics (idempotent producers plus transactional writes) guarantee exactly-once delivery within the scope of producer-to-topic and, with Kafka Streams/ksqlDB transactions, from topic-to-topic -- but that guarantee stops at the boundary of Kafka itself. The moment a consumer reads a record and writes it to an external sink (a database, an API call, a file), you're outside Kafka's transactional guarantee, and that write can fail, retry, or duplicate independently of what Kafka thinks happened, so end-to-end exactly-once across a multi-team, multi-sink chain is not something Kafka hands you for free -- it has to be engineered at every hop where ownership changes. What I'd require of each team: first, consumer offsets must be committed atomically with the downstream write, not before or after it as a separate step, usually by using the sink's own transactional capability (a database transaction that writes both the business data and the committed offset) or an idempotent-write pattern keyed on the event's unique ID so a replay produces the same end state rather than a duplicate. Second, every downstream write must be idempotent by design -- upserts keyed on a stable event ID, not blind inserts -- because at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing is the realistic, achievable target, not literal exactly-once delivery. Third, I'd mandate a dead-letter and replay strategy with monitoring on consumer lag and reprocessing rate, since 'effectively exactly-once' is a property you have to continuously verify, not one you can certify once and forget, especially as teams change their sink implementations independently.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by correcting the framing, because 'Kafka gives you exactly-once' is true, but only for a narrower slice of this chain than people assume. Inside Kafka -- producer to topic, even stream-processor to stream-processor with transactions -- yes, that's solid. The second a team's consumer writes out to its own database or calls an external API, that guarantee is gone, because that write is now that team's problem, not Kafka's. So rather than chase a literal end-to-end exactly-once guarantee across three independently-owned systems, which I don't think is realistically achievable, I'd set a standard every team has to meet: your downstream write has to be idempotent -- keyed on the event's own ID, so if the same event gets delivered twice, the second write is a no-op, not a duplicate -- and your offset commit has to happen atomically with that write, not as a separate step that can drift out of sync with it. That combination, at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, gets you the same practical outcome as exactly-once without requiring a guarantee Kafka can't actually extend across three teams' separate sinks. I'd also insist on dead-letter handling and lag monitoring for each hop, because this isn't a property you verify once at launch -- it's something that can quietly break the next time a team changes how their sink writes data.
commonMistakes: Assumes Kafka's exactly-once guarantee extends automatically to external sinks
Doesn't require idempotent downstream writes keyed on a stable event ID
Commits consumer offsets as a separate step from the downstream write instead of atomically
Treats exactly-once as a one-time certification rather than something to continuously monitor
No dead-letter/replay strategy for the inevitable failure cases
keyPoints: Correctly scopes Kafka's native exactly-once guarantee to within Kafka itself
Explains why external sink writes break that guarantee at hop boundaries
Requires idempotent downstream writes keyed on event ID as the realistic target
Requires atomic offset-commit-with-write patterns per team
Mandates ongoing monitoring (lag, dead-letter) rather than one-time verification

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes where Kafka's exactly-once guarantee actually applies
Proposes idempotent-write and atomic-offset-commit requirements
Recognizes effectively-exactly-once as the realistic, achievable target
Includes ongoing monitoring/verification, not one-time certification

questions.title: dbt Mesh and Cross-Project ref(): Governing Dependencies Without Freezing Teams
questions.prompt: Your analytics engineering org has grown to 12 independent dbt projects, each owned by a different domain team, and they're starting to informally depend on each other's models by copy-pasting SQL. Explain how dbt Mesh's cross-project ref() and model contracts actually solve this, and the governance you'd put around who can depend on what.
questions.modelAnswer: Copy-pasting SQL across 12 projects is the exact failure mode dbt Mesh's cross-project ref() exists to prevent: instead of a downstream team duplicating (and silently diverging from) an upstream team's model logic, they declare a dependency on that model directly via a cross-project ref(), resolved against the upstream project's published artifacts, so the downstream project always consumes the actual current version of that model rather than a copy frozen at whatever date someone pasted it. The second half of the mechanism is model contracts and versioning: an upstream team marks a model as public and defines a contract (an explicit, enforced schema -- column names and types) and can version that model, so if they need to make a breaking change, they ship it as a new version while downstream consumers keep working against the contract version they built against, rather than breaking silently on the next upstream deploy. The governance layer this enables is what you actually need at 12 teams: only models explicitly marked public with a defined contract are eligible to be depended on cross-project -- that's the API surface -- while every other model stays private to its own project, which stops the free-for-all of teams reaching into each other's internal, unstable models. I'd pair this with an ownership registry (which team owns which public model, and an on-call/support expectation for breaking changes) and a deprecation policy for contract versions, so cross-project dependency becomes a managed interface instead of either total lock-down or the uncontrolled copy-paste sprawl you have today.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening with the copy-pasting is basically teams inventing their own, worse version of an API because they don't have a real one -- they see a model they need, they can't formally depend on it, so they just paste the SQL and now there are two versions of the same logic quietly drifting apart. dbt Mesh's cross-project ref() is literally the fix for that: a downstream project can depend on an upstream model directly, so it always gets the real, current version instead of a frozen copy. The piece that makes this safe to roll out to 12 teams, though, is contracts -- an upstream team has to explicitly mark a model public and lock down its schema before anyone else can depend on it that way, and if they need to change it later, they version it rather than breaking everyone downstream overnight. So the governance conversation I'd have with the 12 teams is: your public, contracted models are now effectively your team's API -- document who owns it, what the support expectation is for a breaking change, and how long you'll support an old version before deprecating it. Everything else stays private to your own project by default. That turns 'teams quietly depending on each other's internals' into something we can actually see, own, and support.

Misses that contracts/versioning are what make cross-project dependency safe, not just ref() alone
Proposes making every model public by default instead of an explicit public/private boundary
No ownership or deprecation policy for public models once they're depended upon
Treats this as a purely technical fix with no governance/ownership component

Explains model contracts and versioning as what makes breaking changes safe
Proposes an explicit public/private boundary rather than exposing every model
Requires an ownership registry and support expectations for public models
Includes a deprecation policy for old contract versions

questions.title: Governing Agentic AI Query Access to the Data Platform
questions.prompt: Multiple teams now want to let LLM-based agents query the data platform directly -- generating and running their own SQL against production schemas, and in some cases summarizing results that may include sensitive data. As platform architect, explain the specific new risks this introduces beyond normal human self-serve BI access, and the governance controls you'd require before approving it.
questions.modelAnswer: An AI agent generating its own SQL introduces risks that human self-serve BI mostly doesn't: it can generate a query a human analyst would never think to write, including ones that inadvertently join across tables in a way that re-identifies anonymized data, or ones that scan far more data than intended because the agent has no intuition for cost or blast radius; it can be prompt-injected by data it reads mid-session (a comment field, a support ticket) into running an unintended follow-up query; and unlike a human, it may paraphrase or summarize sensitive fields into an output surface -- a chat response, a generated report -- without the same instinctive judgment a trained analyst has about what's appropriate to surface. The controls I'd require before approving this: first, every agent must run under its own scoped service identity with row/column-level security enforced at the platform layer (via the warehouse's native governance, not client-side filtering an agent could bypass), never under a human's broader credentials, so the agent genuinely cannot see what it isn't entitled to regardless of what it's prompted to do. Second, a hard allowlist of queryable objects (specifically semantic views or governed marts, not raw production tables) so an agent's generated SQL operates against a vetted, already-masked surface rather than schema it could misuse. Third, mandatory query logging and cost/row-scanned limits per agent session, since an agent has no instinct for 'this query is too expensive or too broad' the way an experienced analyst does. Fourth, I'd explicitly prohibit sending any row-level sensitive data to a third-party LLM API as part of the query/response loop -- that has to stay within the platform's own governed boundary, or go through a reviewed, contractually-covered enterprise agreement, never a default API call.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this request with real caution, not because AI-on-data is a bad idea, but because an agent generating its own SQL is a genuinely different risk profile than a human analyst clicking through a BI tool. A human has intuition about what a weird join might expose or how expensive a query looks before running it; an agent doesn't, and it can also be steered by something it reads mid-session, like a comment field with hidden instructions in it, into running a query nobody intended. So before I'd approve this, I'd want the agent running under its own tightly scoped identity, with row and column security enforced by the warehouse itself, not some filter the agent's own code is supposed to respect -- because if it can be prompted around, it will be eventually. I'd also restrict what it's even allowed to query to a governed, already-masked semantic layer, not raw production schemas, so there's a hard ceiling on what a bad or manipulated query could ever expose. And the one thing I'd be absolutely firm on: no sensitive row-level data goes to a third-party LLM API as part of generating or explaining a query result unless we have a specific, reviewed enterprise agreement covering exactly that -- that's not a judgment call I'll let an individual team make on their own.
commonMistakes: Treats agentic AI query access as equivalent in risk to human self-serve BI
Relies on client-side or prompt-level restrictions instead of platform-enforced row/column security
Allows agents to query raw production schemas instead of a governed, masked semantic layer
No logging, cost, or scan-size limits specific to agent-generated queries
No explicit policy preventing sensitive data from being sent to third-party LLM APIs
keyPoints: Identifies agent-specific risks: unintuitive joins, prompt injection, no cost/blast-radius judgment
Requires platform-enforced (not client-side) row/column security under a scoped agent identity
Restricts agent queries to a governed semantic layer, not raw production tables
Mandates logging and resource limits specific to agent sessions
Explicitly prohibits sending sensitive data to third-party LLM APIs without a reviewed agreement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies risks specific to agentic query access vs. human BI
Requires platform-enforced governance rather than client-side controls
Restricts query surface to a governed/masked layer
Sets a clear policy on third-party LLM data exposure

questions.title: Publishing a Governed Public Model with dbt Mesh Contracts
questions.prompt: Write the dbt configuration that turns an internal 'customer_ltv' model into a governed, versioned public model other domain teams can safely depend on via cross-project ref(), and show the downstream project's dependency on it. Explain what breaks for downstream consumers if you change a contracted column's type without bumping the version.
questions.code:
# models/marts/customer_ltv.yml (upstream project: 'finance_core')
models:
  - name: customer_ltv
    access: public
    latest_version: 2
    config:
      contract:
        enforced: true
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: string
        constraints:
          - type: not_null
      - name: ltv_usd
        data_type: numeric(18,2)
      - name: ltv_tier
        data_type: string
    versions:
      - v: 1
        defined_in: customer_ltv_v1
      - v: 2
        defined_in: customer_ltv

# models/marts/marketing_segments.sql (downstream project: 'marketing_analytics')
# dependencies.yml declares the upstream project reference
select
    c.customer_id,
    c.ltv_tier,
    s.segment_name
from {{ ref('finance_core', 'customer_ltv', v=2) }} as c
join {{ ref('segments') }} as s on s.customer_id = c.customer_id
questions.modelAnswer: Publishing a safe public model takes three deliberate choices, not just adding ref(). First, access: public is what makes the model eligible for cross-project reference at all -- every other model in the project defaults to private/protected and can't be depended on this way, which is the actual governance boundary. Second, contract.enforced: true forces dbt to validate that the model's actual output matches the declared column names and types at build time, so a silent schema drift fails the build loudly in the upstream project rather than silently breaking every downstream consumer's queries. Third, versions let the upstream team ship a breaking change (renaming a column, changing a type, changing grain) as a new version while customer_ltv_v1 keeps serving exactly what it always has, so a downstream project pinned to v=1 via ref('finance_core', 'customer_ltv', v=1) is completely unaffected until it deliberately migrates to v=2. If you changed ltv_usd's type without bumping the version, the contract check itself would fail the upstream build the moment the actual column type diverges from the declared contract -- that's the safety net doing its job, forcing you to either fix the model to match the contract or bump the version, rather than letting a breaking change ship silently to every downstream team that depends on it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain this to a team publishing their first public model: access: public isn't just a label, it's the switch that makes your model part of your project's actual API surface, so don't flip it on anything you're not ready to support. The contract is what makes that API trustworthy -- it's a promise about column names and types that dbt actually checks at build time, so if your model's real output ever drifts from what you promised, your own build fails before it can quietly break someone else's downstream job. And versioning is what lets you evolve that promise without breaking the people depending on you -- ship v2 with the new shape, leave v1 running unchanged for anyone still pinned to it, and let teams migrate on their own schedule instead of you forcing an overnight breaking change on them. If you skip the version bump and just change a contracted column's type, you don't get a quiet downstream failure three weeks later -- you get an immediate, loud build failure on your own side, because the contract check catches the mismatch before it ships. That's the whole point of the mechanism: it moves the pain of a breaking change to the moment you make it, not to whoever's downstream.
commonMistakes: Adds cross-project ref() without marking the upstream model access: public
Skips contract.enforced, losing the build-time schema safety net entirely
Changes a contracted column's type or removes a column without bumping the model version
Doesn't pin downstream ref() calls to a specific version, inheriting unplanned breaking changes
Assumes versioning requires maintaining separate physical tables indefinitely rather than deprecating old versions on a schedule
keyPoints: Correctly sets access: public as the cross-project dependency boundary
Enforces a contract to catch schema drift at build time
Uses versioning to ship breaking changes without breaking existing consumers
Shows the downstream project pinning to a specific version via ref()
Explains the contract-check failure mode when a type changes without a version bump

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working dbt Mesh configuration (access, contract, versions)
Correct downstream cross-project ref() usage
Accurately explains the contract-enforcement failure mode
Explains versioning as the mechanism for safe breaking changes

questions.title: A Terraform Module Layout for a Multi-Team, Multi-Environment Data Platform
questions.prompt: Design and write the Terraform module structure and remote-state layout for a platform shared by 15 data teams, each needing isolated dev/staging/prod environments, without a single shared state file becoming a bottleneck or a blast-radius risk. Show the key file layout and one module's backend configuration.
questions.code:
# Repo layout
# modules/
#   data-platform-team/        <- reusable module: one team's resources (storage, warehouse role, ingestion infra)
# environments/
#   dev/
#     teamA/main.tf
#     teamB/main.tf
#   staging/
#     teamA/main.tf
#   prod/
#     teamA/main.tf

# environments/prod/teamA/main.tf
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "tfstate-rg"
    storage_account_name = "platformtfstate"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "prod/teamA.tfstate"   # one state file per team per environment
  }
}

module "team_a_platform" {
  source       = "../../../modules/data-platform-team"
  team_name    = "teamA"
  environment  = "prod"
  owner_tag    = "team-a-data-eng"
  capacity_sku = "F64"
}

# Policy-as-code guardrail applied at plan time (e.g. via OPA/Sentinel/Checkov in CI)
# deny: resource "azurerm_storage_account" without owner_tag or with public network access enabled
questions.modelAnswer: The design decision that matters most here is state isolation: one shared state file across 15 teams and three environments each means every apply touches a state file other teams' infrastructure also lives in, so a bad plan or a stuck lock for one team can block or risk every other team's deploy -- that's an unacceptable blast radius at this scale. The fix is one state file per team per environment (45 state files, not one), each pointed at its own backend key, so team isolation is enforced structurally, not by convention or discipline. On top of that, a single reusable module (data-platform-team) defines what 'a team's platform footprint' means once, and every team/environment combination just calls that module with different input variables -- this is what prevents 15 teams from hand-rolling 15 slightly different, unreviewed infrastructure patterns, while still giving each one isolated state and blast radius. Module ownership itself needs a clear answer: the platform team owns and versions the shared module, while each data team owns its own environment folder and the variables feeding it, so a module change goes through platform-team review while day-to-day variable changes (scaling a capacity SKU, adding a resource) don't require platform-team involvement for every routine change. Policy-as-code guardrails (OPA, Sentinel, or Checkov in CI) enforce non-negotiables -- required tags, no public network exposure, approved SKU tiers -- at plan time, so self-service doesn't mean ungoverned; a team can self-serve within guardrails the platform team controls centrally, catching violations before apply rather than after an incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: The single biggest thing I'd fix before writing a line of actual resource config is state isolation. If 15 teams share one Terraform state file across three environments, I've basically built a system where team B's bad apply can lock or break team A's prod deploy, and that's not a hypothetical, that's a Tuesday. So the layout is one state file per team per environment -- 45 of them -- each with its own backend key, so blast radius is structurally contained rather than something everyone has to be careful about. Then, instead of letting 15 teams each write their own version of 'provision my team's platform footprint,' I'd put that logic in one shared module the platform team owns and versions, and every team/environment folder just calls it with different inputs. That gets me consistency without forcing every team through a ticket for routine changes -- they can bump their own variables and apply within their own isolated state, but if they need a new capability, that's a module change, which goes through platform-team review. And because self-service without guardrails turns into its own kind of incident, I'd run policy-as-code checks in CI -- required owner tags, no public network exposure, approved SKU tiers -- so a violation gets caught at plan time, in a PR, not discovered during an audit six months later.

Lets each team hand-write its own infrastructure code instead of a shared, versioned module
No clear ownership split between the shared module (platform team) and environment config (data teams)
No policy-as-code enforcement, relying on manual review or convention for guardrails
Conflates environment separation with team separation, missing that both dimensions need isolated state

Uses one reusable, versioned module instead of per-team hand-rolled config
Defines a clear ownership split: platform team owns the module, data teams own their environment inputs
Enforces guardrails via policy-as-code at plan time, not manual review
Shows correct, working Terraform backend and module-call syntax

questions.title: Schema Registry Compatibility Mode and Topic ACLs for a Multi-Team Kafka Backbone
questions.prompt: Design the Schema Registry compatibility setting and topic-level ACL structure for a Kafka cluster that's becoming the org-wide event backbone across 10 producing teams and 20+ consuming services. Show the concrete configuration and explain what failure each compatibility mode and ACL choice is actually preventing.
questions.code:
# Schema Registry: set per-subject, default org-wide to BACKWARD
curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"compatibility": "BACKWARD"}' \
  http://schema-registry:8081/config/orders-value

# Topic ACLs (Kafka CLI) - producing team owns write access to its own topic
kafka-acls --bootstrap-server broker:9092 \
  --add --allow-principal User:orders-service \
  --operation Write --operation Describe \
  --topic orders.events

# Consuming teams get Read-only, never Write, on topics they don't own
kafka-acls --bootstrap-server broker:9092 \
  --add --allow-principal User:fraud-detection-consumer \
  --operation Read --operation Describe \
  --topic orders.events --group fraud-detection-group

# Naming convention enforced by policy: <domain>.<entity>.<version> e.g. orders.events.v1
questions.modelAnswer: BACKWARD compatibility (a new schema version can read data written with the previous version) is the right org-wide default because it protects the thing that actually breaks consumers in practice: a producer deploying a schema change that an already-running consumer, built against the old schema, can no longer parse -- BACKWARD compatibility rejects that registration at the Schema Registry before it ever reaches a topic, turning a production incident into a rejected CI step. I'd reserve FORWARD or FULL compatibility only for specific subjects where a documented use case genuinely requires it (an old consumer must read new-schema data, e.g., during a staged consumer rollout), rather than making it the default, because FULL is more restrictive than most teams need and slows down legitimate evolution. For ACLs, the core principle is that only the owning producer gets Write access to its own topic -- every other team, no matter how trusted, gets Read-only, which is what actually prevents the predictable failure mode of a well-meaning downstream team 'fixing' upstream data by writing directly into someone else's topic and silently corrupting the event stream for every other consumer. Consumer groups are also scoped per-service rather than shared, so one team's consumer can't accidentally commit offsets that affect another team's independent read position on the same topic. A mandatory topic-naming convention (domain.entity.version) isn't cosmetic -- it's what makes ACL policy itself enforceable and auditable at 10+ producing teams, since without it you can't write a consistent ACL or ownership rule at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The compatibility setting I'd default the whole org to is BACKWARD, because the failure it's protecting against is the one that actually happens: someone on a producing team changes their schema, deploys it, and three consuming services they've never talked to start throwing parse errors in production because they were built against the old shape. BACKWARD compatibility catches that at registration time, in the Schema Registry, before it ever becomes a live incident -- the bad schema change just gets rejected with a clear error, which is a much better place for that failure to happen than a 2am page. I wouldn't make every topic FULL compatibility by default, though -- that's more restrictive than most teams need and it'll just generate friction for legitimate, safe schema evolution; I'd reserve stricter modes for the specific topics where there's a real documented reason, like a staged consumer migration. On ACLs, the rule I hold the line on is: you get write access to your own topic, full stop, and read-only on everyone else's. I've seen what happens when a downstream team gets write access 'just to patch one bad record' -- it becomes a habit, and eventually someone corrupts an upstream event stream that twenty other services depend on. And none of this works at scale without an enforced naming convention, because you genuinely cannot write a sane, auditable ACL policy for an unstructured pile of topic names.
commonMistakes: Defaults every topic to FULL compatibility, creating unnecessary friction for normal schema evolution
Grants write ACLs to consuming teams on topics they don't own
Shares consumer groups across teams instead of scoping them per-service
No enforced topic-naming convention, making ACL policy inconsistent and unauditable
Doesn't distinguish which compatibility mode protects against which specific failure
keyPoints: Chooses BACKWARD as the sane org-wide default compatibility mode
Explains exactly what failure BACKWARD compatibility prevents
Grants write ACLs only to the owning producer; read-only to all other consumers
Scopes consumer groups per-service
Enforces a topic-naming convention that makes governance auditable at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses and justifies a default compatibility mode
Designs a correct, least-privilege ACL structure
Working, accurate configuration/CLI examples
Explains the specific failure each control prevents

questions.title: Resource Monitors and Multi-Cluster Warehouse Config for 40 Self-Serve Teams
questions.prompt: Write the Snowflake SQL to create a warehouse with multi-cluster auto-scaling appropriate for a BI workload with unpredictable concurrency, plus a resource monitor with graduated actions, assigned to that warehouse.
questions.code:
CREATE WAREHOUSE bi_shared_wh
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM'
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
  MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 6
  SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 120
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;

CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR bi_shared_monitor
  WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 500
  FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
  START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS
    ON 50 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
    ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
    ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND
    ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;

ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_shared_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = bi_shared_monitor;
questions.modelAnswer: MEDIUM size with MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT=1, MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT=6, and STANDARD scaling policy is the correct combination for unpredictable BI concurrency specifically because the problem described -- variable numbers of concurrent dashboard queries -- is a concurrency problem, not a per-query performance problem; going bigger on warehouse size would make each individual query faster but do nothing for queueing when many users hit it at once, whereas multi-cluster lets Snowflake add clusters of the same size as concurrent load actually rises and scale back down as it falls, matching cost to real demand rather than provisioning for peak at all times. AUTO_SUSPEND at 120 seconds with AUTO_RESUME ensures idle clusters don't bill when nobody's querying, which matters more as cluster count grows since idle waste multiplies across clusters, not just one warehouse. The resource monitor's graduated triggers are the governance payoff: notifications at 50% and 75% give the team owning this warehouse a chance to intervene or communicate before anything breaks, SUSPEND at 100% stops new queries from starting (letting in-flight ones finish) rather than violently killing active work, and SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 110% is the hard backstop for a genuine runaway scenario where even a graceful suspend wasn't enough. Assigning the monitor via ALTER WAREHOUSE ties the whole cost ceiling to this specific shared warehouse rather than the account globally, which is what lets you run this pattern independently per team or workload across 40 self-serving groups without one team's monitor affecting another's.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a BI warehouse where the issue is unpredictable concurrency, not slow individual queries, I wouldn't reach for a bigger size -- that's solving the wrong problem. I'd set it to a moderate size and let multi-cluster do the actual work: one cluster minimum, up to six if load spikes, standard scaling policy so it adds capacity as concurrent queries pile up and scales back down the moment they don't. Auto-suspend at two minutes keeps us from paying for idle time, which matters even more once you've got up to six clusters that could each be sitting idle. The resource monitor is really the piece that makes this safe to hand to a team self-serving their own warehouse: I don't want them finding out they're over budget from a bill at the end of the month, so they get a heads-up at half and three-quarters of quota, a graceful suspend of new queries at full quota so in-flight work isn't killed mid-run, and a hard immediate stop a bit past that in case something's genuinely gone wrong. Tying that monitor to this one warehouse specifically, rather than an account-wide setting, is what lets 40 different teams each run this same safe pattern independently without stepping on each other's budgets.
commonMistakes: Increases warehouse size instead of multi-cluster count to fix a concurrency/queueing problem
Omits AUTO_SUSPEND, leaving idle clusters billing unnecessarily
Sets a single hard SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE trigger with no graduated notify/suspend steps
Uses an account-level resource monitor instead of scoping one per shared warehouse
Incorrect or missing MIN/MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT syntax
keyPoints: Correctly uses multi-cluster scaling (not size) to address concurrency
Sets AUTO_SUSPEND/AUTO_RESUME to avoid idle-cluster cost
Designs graduated resource-monitor triggers (notify, suspend, suspend immediate)
Scopes the resource monitor to this specific warehouse
Produces correct, runnable Snowflake SQL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working SQL for warehouse and resource monitor
Correctly justifies multi-cluster over size for this workload
Designs sensible graduated triggers
Explains auto-suspend's cost impact at multi-cluster scale

questions.title: Row-Level Security Across Unity Catalog for a Multi-Tenant Analytics Table
questions.prompt: Write the Unity Catalog SQL to enforce row-level security on a shared 'orders' table so each of several enterprise customers (tenants) can only see their own rows through self-serve SQL/BI access, using a row filter function and grants.
questions.modelAnswer: The row filter function is the actual enforcement mechanism: once attached to the table via ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER, Unity Catalog evaluates it for every query against that table, transparently rewriting the query to apply the filter -- a tenant's BI tool running a plain SELECT * never sees rows outside its own tenant_id, and critically, it can't be bypassed by querying differently, because the filter is enforced at the storage/query-planning layer, not in application code that a clever query could route around. The IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER check inside the function is what lets platform admins still see everything for support and debugging, while every ordinary tenant session gets filtered to current_user_tenant() -- resolving the caller's tenant from a mapping table keyed on their authenticated principal, rather than trusting a client-supplied tenant_id parameter that a user could simply change. The GRANT SELECT on the underlying table is still necessary and separate from the row filter: the grant controls whether a principal can query the table at all, while the row filter controls which rows they see once they can -- conflating these (relying on the grant alone) would mean anyone granted access sees every tenant's rows, defeating the entire point of a shared multi-tenant table. This pattern scales to hundreds of tenants without any per-tenant schema or table proliferation, because the isolation lives in one row filter function and one mapping table, not in infrastructure.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key thing to get right here is that a GRANT and a row filter are solving two different problems, and people sometimes think granting access is enough -- it isn't. The grant says 'this role can query the orders table at all'; the row filter is what actually decides which rows they see once they're in. So I attach a row filter function to the table that looks up the calling user's tenant from a mapping table -- never from something the client passes in, because that's trivially spoofable -- and compares it against each row's tenant_id, letting platform admins through as an explicit exception for support work. Once that's attached, it doesn't matter how creatively a tenant's BI tool writes its query; Unity Catalog is rewriting every query against that table to respect the filter underneath, so there's no clever SELECT that gets around it. What I like about this pattern at scale is that it doesn't require a table or schema per tenant -- one shared table, one filter function, one mapping table, and it holds whether you've got five tenants or five hundred.
commonMistakes: Relies on a client-supplied tenant_id parameter instead of resolving tenant from an authenticated server-side mapping
Assumes GRANT SELECT alone provides row-level isolation
Omits an admin/support bypass, making debugging and operations impossible
Proposes a separate table or schema per tenant instead of a shared table with a row filter
Incorrect or non-functional SQL for the row filter function or ALTER TABLE statement
keyPoints: Correctly uses a row filter function attached via ALTER TABLE SET ROW FILTER
Resolves tenant identity server-side from an authenticated mapping, not a client parameter
Distinguishes GRANT (can query) from row filter (which rows), and uses both correctly
Includes an explicit, auditable admin bypass
Scales to many tenants without table/schema proliferation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working row filter SQL
Resolves tenant identity securely, not via a spoofable client parameter
Correctly distinguishes and uses both grants and row filters
Includes a sound admin/support bypass

questions.title: A Fabric Deployment Pipeline for Promoting Dozens of Items Across Environments
questions.prompt: Write the CI/CD configuration (using Fabric's deployment pipelines plus a Git-integrated workspace) that promotes a set of Fabric items -- notebooks, a semantic model, a data pipeline -- from dev to test to prod with environment-specific parameter overrides, and explain how you'd prevent an untested item from reaching prod.
questions.code:
# .github/workflows/fabric-promote.yml
name: fabric-promote
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy workspace to Test stage
        run: |
          fab api -X POST "deploymentPipelines/${{ vars.PIPELINE_ID }}/deploy" \
            --body '{"sourceStageId": "${{ vars.DEV_STAGE_ID }}", "targetStageId": "${{ vars.TEST_STAGE_ID }}"}'
      - name: Apply test-stage parameter overrides
        run: |
          fab set-param --stage test --lakehouse-connection "test_lakehouse" --capacity "F8"

  deploy-prod:
    needs: deploy-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # requires manual approval gate configured in repo settings
    steps:
      - name: Deploy workspace to Prod stage
        run: |
          fab api -X POST "deploymentPipelines/${{ vars.PIPELINE_ID }}/deploy" \
            --body '{"sourceStageId": "${{ vars.TEST_STAGE_ID }}", "targetStageId": "${{ vars.PROD_STAGE_ID }}"}'
      - name: Apply prod-stage parameter overrides
        run: |
          fab set-param --stage prod --lakehouse-connection "prod_lakehouse" --capacity "F64"
questions.modelAnswer: A Fabric deployment pipeline's three stages (dev/test/prod) map Git-integrated workspace content forward, and the piece that makes this safe rather than just convenient is deployment rules: per-stage parameter overrides (like the lakehouse connection string and capacity SKU shown here) that are configured once, per target stage, so promoting an item doesn't require anyone to manually edit a connection string by hand in prod and risk pointing a production pipeline at a test lakehouse by mistake. To prevent an untested item reaching prod, the control that actually matters is a required, non-bypassable approval gate between the test and prod deploy steps -- shown here as a GitHub Actions `environment: production` protection rule -- so a human has to explicitly approve promotion after confirming test-stage validation passed, rather than the pipeline auto-cascading dev through to prod on every merge. I'd pair that gate with a concrete, automated test-stage validation step (data quality checks, a smoke-test notebook run, semantic model refresh success) that has to pass before the approval gate is even presented, so the human approver is confirming a verified signal, not just rubber-stamping based on 'it looked fine in dev.' Git integration on the workspace is what gives you the audit trail and rollback capability underneath all of this -- every promoted change traces back to a specific commit, so a bad prod deploy can be rolled back to a known-good commit rather than manually reconstructed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part of this that actually prevents an untested item from reaching prod isn't the pipeline mechanics, it's the approval gate between test and prod -- I make that a real, enforced gate, not just a step someone could skip by running a different script. In GitHub Actions that's an environment protection rule requiring a specific person or team to click approve; in Azure DevOps it's an equivalent manual approval check. Before that gate even shows up, I want an automated validation step to have run and passed in the test stage -- data quality checks, a smoke test on the notebook, confirming the semantic model actually refreshes -- so whoever's approving is looking at a real pass/fail signal, not just vibes. The parameter overrides are what keep this from becoming a manual, error-prone process at each stage -- the pipeline knows prod points at the prod lakehouse and the F64 capacity, test points at its own lakehouse and a smaller capacity, and nobody's hand-editing a connection string in a production workspace at 5pm on a Friday. And because the whole workspace is Git-integrated, if something does slip through, I'm not reconstructing what changed from memory -- I'm looking at a commit history and rolling back to the last known-good one.

Doesn't use Git integration, losing audit trail and rollback capability
Treats test-stage success as optional rather than a required gate before prod promotion

questions.title: Cross-DAG Dependencies and Ownership Tags Across a Multi-Team Airflow Estate
questions.prompt: Write an Airflow DAG that depends on another team's upstream DAG finishing successfully, with an SLA, clear ownership metadata, and a cross-DAG sensor that doesn't poll so aggressively it degrades the metadata database at hundreds of DAGs scale.
questions.code:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.sensors.external_task import ExternalTaskSensor
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

default_args = {
    "owner": "marketing-analytics-team",
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5),
    "sla": timedelta(hours=2),
}

with DAG(
    dag_id="marketing_segment_refresh",
    default_args=default_args,
    schedule="0 6 * * *",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
    tags=["owner:marketing-analytics", "domain:marketing", "depends-on:orders-core"],
) as dag:

    wait_for_orders_core = ExternalTaskSensor(
        task_id="wait_for_orders_core",
        external_dag_id="orders_core_ingestion",
        external_task_id="publish_orders_mart",
        allowed_states=["success"],
        failed_states=["failed", "skipped"],
        mode="reschedule",       # frees the worker slot between pokes instead of holding it
        poke_interval=300,        # 5 minutes, not aggressive polling
        timeout=60 * 60 * 3,      # fail loudly after 3 hours rather than hang indefinitely
    )

    def refresh_segments():
        pass  # real segment-build logic

    build_segments = PythonOperator(task_id="build_segments", python_callable=refresh_segments)

    wait_for_orders_core >> build_segments
questions.modelAnswer: mode='reschedule' is the detail that matters most at hundreds-of-DAGs scale: the default mode='poke' holds a worker slot for the entire wait duration, so if dozens of downstream DAGs are all waiting on upstream dependencies simultaneously, you can exhaust worker capacity on pure waiting rather than actual work; reschedule releases the slot between poke intervals and only re-acquires one when it's actually time to check again, which is what keeps a large cross-team DAG estate from starving itself on sensors alone. A 5-minute poke_interval is deliberately not aggressive -- checking every few seconds would hammer the metadata database with scheduler queries across potentially hundreds of similar sensors, while 5 minutes is more than fine for a dependency that completes on an hours-long cadence; the right interval scales with how time-sensitive the dependency actually is, not a reflexive default. The explicit timeout ensures the sensor fails loudly after a bounded wait instead of hanging indefinitely if the upstream DAG never runs or silently fails in a way the sensor's allowed_states/failed_states don't immediately catch -- a silent, indefinitely-waiting DAG is a much worse failure mode than one that pages someone after three hours. The ownership tag and 'depends-on' tag in the DAG's tags aren't cosmetic: at hundreds of DAGs across many teams, being able to query 'which DAGs does this one depend on, and who owns them' without manually reading source code is what makes a cross-team outage actually triageable instead of requiring whoever's on-call to read every team's code to find the dependency chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The one change that matters most for the metadata database's health at scale is using mode='reschedule' instead of the default 'poke.' Poke mode holds a worker slot the entire time it's waiting, so if you've got a hundred DAGs across different teams all waiting on various upstream dependencies at the same time, you can genuinely run yourself out of worker capacity just from sensors sitting there waiting, not doing anything. Reschedule gives that slot back between checks, which is the difference between a sensor being nearly free and a sensor quietly eating your scheduler's capacity. I also don't poll every few seconds just because I can -- a 5-minute interval is plenty for something that only finishes once a day, and hammering the metadata DB with constant poke queries across hundreds of similar sensors is exactly the kind of thing that degrades scheduler performance for every team, not just mine. The timeout matters too -- I'd rather this DAG fail loudly after three hours and page someone than hang forever because the upstream team's DAG silently died in a state my sensor isn't watching for. And the tags aren't decoration -- when there's an incident at 2am, 'owner:marketing-analytics, depends-on:orders-core' tells whoever's on-call exactly who to loop in without reading anyone's source code.

Sets an aggressive poke_interval that generates excessive load on the metadata database across many DAGs
Omits a timeout, allowing the sensor to hang indefinitely on a silently failed or never-running upstream
No ownership or dependency metadata, making cross-team incident triage require reading source code
Doesn't specify failed_states, so an upstream failure isn't detected as distinctly as a success

Sets a reasonable, non-aggressive poke_interval appropriate to the dependency's cadence
Sets an explicit timeout so the sensor fails loudly rather than hanging forever
Includes ownership and dependency tags for cross-team triage
Produces a correct, working Airflow DAG
