questions.title: Rewriting an Isolation-Level-Dependent Procedure for a Cross-Dialect Migration
questions.prompt: This T-SQL procedure relies on SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED locking behavior and an explicit transaction to prevent a double-booking race condition on a limited-inventory reservation. Rewrite it for a target dialect (PostgreSQL) that defaults to MVCC-based read committed, preserving the same correctness guarantee, and explain exactly what would break if you migrated it line-for-line without this change.
questions.modelAnswer: A line-for-line migration would break because the original procedure's correctness isn't actually guaranteed by its explicit transaction -- it's guaranteed by an implicit side effect of SQL Server's default READ COMMITTED locking behavior, where the SELECT inside the transaction takes a shared lock that blocks a concurrent writer from updating QtyAvailable until this transaction commits or rolls back, closing the race between the check and the update. PostgreSQL's default read committed is MVCC-based, not lock-based in the same way: a plain SELECT never blocks a concurrent UPDATE, so two simultaneous callers can both read the same QtyAvailable, both see enough inventory, and both proceed to update -- a classic check-then-act race that silently double-books the last unit of inventory, with no error raised anywhere. Migrating this procedure correctly requires recognizing that the original's safety was a side effect of platform-specific locking semantics, not a property of its logic, and then re-architecting the logic itself to be safe under the target platform's actual concurrency model -- here, collapsing the check and the update into a single atomic statement (UPDATE ... WHERE qty_available >= p_qty) so PostgreSQL's row-level locking on the UPDATE itself, not a separate read, is what prevents the race: the second concurrent caller's UPDATE simply affects zero rows once the first has already decremented past the threshold, and ROW_COUNT tells the caller whether the reservation actually succeeded. This is exactly the category of migration risk that a pure syntax-translation tool would never catch, because the original SQL is syntactically valid and 'looks correct' on both platforms -- it just isn't equally correct on both.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the kind of bug that a migration tool translating syntax would sail right past, because the original procedure looks completely correct -- it reads the available quantity, checks it, updates it, all inside a transaction. The problem is that its actual safety doesn't come from the transaction, it comes from a side effect of how SQL Server locks reads under its default isolation level: that SELECT takes a shared lock that happens to block a concurrent writer. PostgreSQL's MVCC-based read committed doesn't do that -- a SELECT there never blocks a concurrent UPDATE -- so if you migrated this line for line, two people could both read 'five available,' both think they're fine to take the last unit, and both successfully update, and now you've sold inventory that doesn't exist with zero error anywhere in the logs. My fix is to stop relying on a read-then-write pattern at all and collapse it into one atomic UPDATE with the quantity check in the WHERE clause -- now the row-level lock PostgreSQL takes during the UPDATE itself is what closes the race, and I check the row count afterward to know whether the reservation actually went through. This is exactly why I don't trust a migration that 'compiled and looks the same' -- the real risk in cross-dialect migrations isn't syntax, it's logic that was only correct because of an implicit platform behavior nobody wrote down anywhere.
commonMistakes: Migrates the procedure line-for-line, assuming the explicit transaction alone guarantees the same safety on PostgreSQL
Doesn't recognize that the original's correctness depended on SQL Server's locking-read behavior, not the transaction boundary itself
Proposes SERIALIZABLE isolation as the fix instead of the simpler, cheaper atomic UPDATE pattern
Fails to check ROW_COUNT/affected rows to determine if the reservation actually succeeded
Assumes a procedure that 'looks the same' in both dialects behaves the same under concurrency
keyPoints: Correctly identifies that the original's safety depended on SQL Server's default locking-read behavior
Explains why PostgreSQL's MVCC read committed does not provide the same implicit protection
Rewrites the logic as a single atomic UPDATE with the condition in the WHERE clause
Checks affected row count to determine reservation success
Frames this as the real risk category in cross-dialect migrations beyond syntax translation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the platform-specific locking assumption in the original code
Correct, race-free rewritten PostgreSQL implementation
Explains precisely what breaks under a naive line-for-line migration
Generalizes the lesson to cross-dialect migration risk

questions.title: Enforcing a Data Contract in CI Before It Reaches the Shared Platform
questions.prompt: Write a JSON Schema data contract for an 'orders.events' topic and the CI check logic that validates a producing team's sample payload against it before their change can merge, including how you'd fail a pull request on a breaking change versus allow a backward-compatible addition.
questions.modelAnswer: The mechanism that actually distinguishes a breaking change from a safe addition is validating the new sample payload against the OLD contract, not just validating it against the new one -- if a sample payload that represents the producer's intended new output still satisfies the previous contract, the change is additive/backward-compatible (a new optional field, a widened enum) and can merge automatically; if it fails the old contract (a required field removed, a type changed, an enum value removed that a consumer may depend on), that's a breaking change by definition, and the CI check fails the PR unless someone explicitly acknowledges it via a label or flag, forcing a conscious decision rather than an accidental breaking deploy. additionalProperties: false is doing real governance work here too: without it, a producer could silently add fields forever with no contract enforcement at all, which defeats the purpose of having a contract -- every field a producer wants to add has to be declared, reviewed, and versioned, even if adding it is backward-compatible. This CI check is deliberately placed before merge, not after deploy, because the entire value of a data contract is catching the break at the cheapest possible point -- a rejected PR -- rather than the most expensive one, which is twenty downstream consumers failing in production because a producer's schema changed underneath them with no warning.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trick to actually telling a safe change from a breaking one in CI is simple but easy to miss: you don't just check the new payload against the new schema, you check it against the old one too. If a sample of what the producer wants to ship still passes the old contract, it's additive and safe to merge automatically -- you added an optional field, you widened an enum, nothing downstream breaks. If it fails the old contract, that's a breaking change by definition, whether or not the producer meant it to be, and I want that PR to fail loudly with a clear list of what broke, not merge quietly and become next week's incident. I do let people override that with an explicit 'breaking-change-approved' flag, but it has to be a deliberate choice someone makes, tied to actually coordinating with downstream consumers, not something that happens by accident because nobody noticed the diff. And I lock down additionalProperties to false on purpose -- otherwise the contract is really just documentation, since a producer could tack on whatever fields they want with no enforcement at all. The whole point of putting this check in CI, before merge, is that a rejected pull request costs five minutes; the same mistake reaching twenty consumers in production costs a week and a trust problem with every team depending on this topic.
commonMistakes: Only validates the new payload against the new schema, missing the actual breaking-change detection
Allows additionalProperties to remain unrestricted, making the contract unenforceable
No explicit override/approval mechanism for intentional breaking changes
Runs the contract check after deploy instead of as a pre-merge CI gate
Doesn't fail the build on a detected breaking change, only warns
keyPoints: Validates the new sample payload against the OLD contract to detect breaking changes
Requires explicit approval to merge an intentional breaking change
Locks down additionalProperties to make the contract actually enforceable
Places the check in CI, before merge, not after deploy
Produces a correct, working JSON Schema and CI check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct backward-compatibility detection logic (validate against old contract)
Correct, working JSON Schema and CI script
Requires explicit approval for intentional breaking changes
Places the gate pre-merge rather than post-deploy

questions.title: DR Failover Serves Stale Data Because of Unnoticed Replication Lag
questions.prompt: Your platform failed over to its secondary region during a real regional outage, and it worked -- traffic kept flowing. Two hours later, finance discovers that several reports produced during the failover window showed numbers that didn't match reality, because the secondary region's replica was lagging the primary by several minutes at the moment of failover. Walk through how you'd diagnose the actual lag at the moment of the incident, and the durable fixes you'd put in place.
questions.modelAnswer: The failover itself succeeded on the metric everyone was watching -- availability -- while silently failing on a metric nobody was watching at the moment: replication lag at the instant of cutover. To diagnose after the fact, I'd pull the replication lag time series for the exact failover window from whatever the platform's replication mechanism exposes (binlog/WAL position lag, a managed service's replica-lag metric), correlate it against the exact timestamp the failover was triggered, and identify which specific tables or topics were how many seconds or minutes behind -- this tells you precisely which downstream reports, covering which time window, are untrustworthy, rather than guessing or distrusting everything produced during the incident. The durable fixes operate at two different layers: first, the failover runbook/automation itself should check current replication lag before promoting the secondary and either block automatic promotion above a defined lag threshold (forcing a conscious risk decision rather than a silent one) or, if availability requirements demand immediate failover regardless of lag, it should emit a clear, automated 'promoted with N seconds of lag, data may be stale until caught up' signal that flows to downstream consumers and dashboards, not just an ops log nobody reads during an active incident. Second, I'd add a continuous, alerting-backed SLO on replication lag itself (not just replica up/down health), so lag growing toward dangerous levels is caught and addressed long before any failover is needed, and I'd add a post-failover reconciliation step that automatically flags or recomputes any report/aggregate whose underlying data window overlapped a period of elevated lag, rather than relying on finance to notice the numbers look wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd tell the team first is that the failover didn't actually fail -- it did exactly what it was built to do, keep the lights on -- but we only instrumented and alerted on availability, not on whether the data we were serving during that window was actually current. So step one is diagnosis: pull the replication lag metric for the exact failover window, line it up against the cutover timestamp, and get a precise answer to 'which tables, for how many minutes, were behind' -- that turns 'some reports looked wrong' into a specific, bounded list of what needs to be flagged or recomputed, instead of everyone distrusting every report from that day. Longer term, I'd put a lag check directly into the failover decision itself: if lag's above a threshold when a failover is triggered, either hold the promotion and surface that explicitly to on-call, or promote anyway but make the staleness visible everywhere downstream immediately, not buried in a log line. And I'd stop treating 'is the replica up' as the only health signal that matters -- lag itself needs its own SLO and alert, so we catch it creeping up well before we ever need to fail over, and a reconciliation job should automatically flag anything computed during a lag spike rather than waiting for finance to spot it two hours later.
commonMistakes: Treats a successful failover as fully successful without checking data currency at the moment of cutover
Has no replication lag metric or SLO separate from basic replica health/uptime
No mechanism to flag or recompute reports/aggregates affected by a lagging failover
Assumes blocking failover on lag is always correct, without weighing availability requirements
Diagnoses the incident qualitatively ('reports looked wrong') instead of pulling exact lag metrics for the window
keyPoints: Diagnoses exact replication lag during the failover window using real metrics, not guesswork
Distinguishes availability success from data-currency failure
Proposes a lag-aware failover decision (block or explicitly flag staleness)
Adds a continuous replication-lag SLO and alert, not just replica-health monitoring
Adds automated post-incident reconciliation/flagging rather than relying on downstream teams to notice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, specific diagnostic approach using real lag metrics
Distinguishes availability from data-currency as separate concerns
Proposes a sound lag-aware failover policy
Proposes durable monitoring and reconciliation fixes

questions.title: A Kafka Consumer Group Caught in a Rebalancing Storm
questions.prompt: A shared Kafka cluster serving 20+ consumer groups starts seeing one consumer group rebalance constantly -- every few minutes -- and consumer lag for that group climbs steadily because it spends more time rebalancing than actually consuming. Diagnose the likely root causes and the fix for each, and explain why this can eventually degrade other consumer groups on the same cluster too.
questions.modelAnswer: A constant rebalance storm almost always traces to one of three causes, and I'd check them in order of likelihood. First, and most common: a consumer's processing loop takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the broker concludes the consumer has died (even though it's just slow) and kicks it out of the group, triggering a rebalance -- the fix is either reducing max.poll.records so each poll does less work per interval, moving heavy per-record processing off the poll thread, or raising max.poll.interval.ms if the processing genuinely needs that long, but only after confirming the consumer is making real progress, not stuck. Second: session.timeout.ms set too aggressively relative to actual network/GC pause behavior, causing the broker to presume a live consumer has died during a transient pause -- widening the timeout (paired with a sane heartbeat.interval.ms) fixes false-positive membership loss without masking a genuinely dead consumer for too long. Third: the consumer group's membership itself is unstable because instances are being killed and restarted frequently (a crash loop, an aggressive autoscaler, a deployment rolling too fast), in which case the rebalancing is a symptom of that instability, not the root cause, and fixing the deploy/autoscaling behavior is the real fix. This degrades other consumer groups on the same cluster because every rebalance requires broker-side coordinator work and, during the rebalance, consumption pauses entirely for that group -- at scale, a group rebalancing every few minutes generates sustained coordinator load and request traffic that competes with the brokers' capacity to service every other group's fetch and commit requests, so one unstable group's churn becomes measurable latency for everyone else.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is almost always the same here: check whether max.poll.interval.ms is being exceeded, because that's the single most common cause of a rebalance storm I've seen, and it's easy to miss because the consumer isn't actually dead, it's just doing too much work per poll and getting declared dead by the broker. If that's it, the fix is usually either doing less work per poll.records or moving heavy processing off that thread entirely. If that's not it, I look at session.timeout.ms next -- if it's tuned aggressively and the consumer has any GC pauses or network blips, the broker will keep deciding it's gone when it isn't, and widening that timeout a bit (with a sensible heartbeat interval alongside it) usually settles it down without hiding a genuinely dead consumer for too long. And if neither of those explains it, I stop looking at consumer config entirely and look at whether the instances themselves are unstable -- getting killed and restarted on a crash loop or an overly aggressive autoscaler -- because then the rebalancing isn't the problem, it's the symptom of something upstream. The reason I push to fix this quickly rather than let it run is that every rebalance has real broker-side coordination cost, and the group pauses consuming entirely while it's happening -- do that every few minutes and you're generating sustained load on the cluster's coordinators that starts showing up as latency for every other group sharing those brokers, not just the one that's unstable.
commonMistakes: Jumps straight to tuning session.timeout.ms without checking max.poll.interval.ms first, which is the more common cause
Doesn't recognize that frequent instance restarts (crash loop, aggressive autoscaling) is often the upstream root cause
Treats the rebalancing as isolated to the affected group, missing the shared-cluster coordinator load impact
Widens timeouts indiscriminately without confirming the consumer is actually making progress
Has no plan to verify the fix actually reduced rebalance frequency, not just masked the symptom
keyPoints: Diagnoses max.poll.interval.ms exceedance as the most common root cause
Considers session.timeout.ms/heartbeat tuning against real pause behavior
Considers consumer instance instability (crash loop, autoscaling) as an upstream root cause
Explains the shared-cluster coordinator-load impact on other consumer groups
Prioritizes diagnosis order by likelihood rather than guessing at one fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the most likely root causes in a sensible order
Proposes correct, specific fixes for each cause
Explains the shared-cluster blast-radius impact on other consumer groups
Verifies the fix rather than assuming it worked

questions.title: The Airflow Scheduler Is Falling Behind Across Hundreds of DAGs
questions.prompt: Your organization's Airflow deployment has grown to 400+ DAGs owned by a dozen teams. Task start times are increasingly delayed relative to their scheduled time, and the gap is growing week over week. Diagnose where the bottleneck actually is, and the architectural changes you'd make, as distinct from quick mitigations.
questions.modelAnswer: At 400+ DAGs, the symptom of 'tasks start late and the gap is growing' is almost always a scheduler throughput problem, not a worker capacity problem, and the first diagnostic step is to separate the two: checking worker/executor queue depth and slot utilization tells you if tasks are queued waiting for an available worker (capacity problem, fixable by scaling workers/executors), while checking scheduler loop duration and DAG-file-parsing time tells you if tasks aren't even being scheduled promptly because the scheduler itself is the bottleneck, which is the more common and more serious cause at this scale. A very common root cause specifically at hundreds of DAGs is DAG-parsing overhead: every scheduler loop re-parses every DAG file to detect changes, and if teams have written DAGs with heavy top-level code (database calls, API calls, or expensive computation executed at parse time rather than inside a task), that cost is paid on every single parse cycle across every DAG, compounding linearly with DAG count. The architectural fixes, distinct from quick mitigations like just adding scheduler replicas: first, enforce a platform-wide standard that DAG top-level code must be cheap -- no network calls, no heavy computation outside of task callables -- enforced via a CI lint check on DAG files before they're allowed to merge, not just a wiki guideline. Second, consider splitting the single Airflow deployment into multiple scheduler/executor pools segmented by team or criticality, so one team's parsing-heavy or task-heavy DAGs can't starve scheduling capacity for every other team's time-sensitive pipelines -- this is the same noisy-neighbor problem you'd solve with workload isolation in any shared platform. Third, tune min_file_process_interval and parsing concurrency settings based on actual measured parse times, and track scheduler loop duration as an explicit platform SLO with alerting, so the degradation is caught and addressed incrementally rather than discovered only once it's already user-visible and widespread.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch any config, I want to know whether this is a worker problem or a scheduler problem, because the fix is completely different depending on which it is -- and at 400-plus DAGs, in my experience it's almost always the scheduler, not worker capacity. I'd check queue depth and slot utilization first just to rule out the simple case, then look at scheduler loop duration and how long DAG file parsing is actually taking, because that's usually where the real bottleneck lives. And the most common cause I've seen at this scale is DAGs with expensive code sitting at the top level of the file instead of inside a task -- a database call or an API call that runs on every single parse cycle, which the scheduler does constantly across every DAG. With 400 DAGs, if even a dozen of them are doing that, you've built a tax that gets paid hundreds of times an hour. So the real fix isn't 'add more scheduler replicas and hope' -- it's getting a CI check in place that fails a PR if a DAG file has anything expensive outside a task callable, so this stops being something we clean up after the fact and becomes something that can't ship in the first place. I'd also look seriously at splitting scheduling capacity by team or criticality, because right now one team's badly-written DAGs can slow down every other team's time-sensitive pipeline, and that's not a config problem, that's a shared-resource isolation problem.
commonMistakes: Assumes the bottleneck is worker/executor capacity without checking scheduler loop duration first
Doesn't identify expensive top-level DAG code as a common root cause at scale
Treats adding scheduler replicas as a complete fix rather than addressing parsing cost directly
No CI/lint enforcement to prevent expensive top-level code from being introduced by new DAGs
No workload isolation between teams, allowing one team's DAGs to degrade scheduling for everyone
keyPoints: Distinguishes worker-capacity bottleneck from scheduler-throughput bottleneck
Identifies expensive top-level DAG parsing code as a likely root cause at scale
Proposes a CI/lint enforcement mechanism, not just a guideline
Considers splitting scheduling capacity/pools by team to prevent noisy-neighbor degradation
Tracks scheduler loop duration as an explicit, alerted platform SLO

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes scheduler vs. worker bottlenecks diagnostically
Identifies expensive DAG parsing as the likely root cause at scale
Proposes durable architectural fixes, not just quick mitigations
Addresses cross-team workload isolation

questions.title: dbt Slim CI Keeps Passing Jobs It Shouldn't
questions.prompt: Your org relies on dbt's Slim CI (state:modified+ comparison against production manifest) to only build and test changed models on pull requests, across 200+ models and multiple dbt projects. You discover a breaking change shipped to production last month that Slim CI should have caught but didn't flag as modified. Diagnose the likely causes of this false negative at scale, and the fixes.
questions.modelAnswer: Slim CI's state comparison only works correctly if the production manifest.json it's comparing against is genuinely current and complete, so the most common root cause of a false negative at this scale is a stale or incomplete reference manifest: if the CI job is pulling a manifest from a production run that predates several other merged changes, or from the wrong project/environment entirely in a multi-project dbt Mesh setup, state:modified+ will correctly compare against the wrong baseline and simply miss changes that happened in between -- the tool isn't broken, it's answering a question against outdated context. Second common cause: the breaking change may have been to something state:modified+ doesn't track as a 'modified' model by default -- a change to a macro, a seed file, a source's freshness definition, or an env var/Jinja context value that affects compiled SQL without changing the model file's own checksum in a way the comparison catches, depending on exact dbt version and configuration; this requires explicitly verifying what the comparison actually covers in the dbt version in use, not assuming it tracks every kind of change a developer might consider 'a change.' Third, in a multi-project Mesh setup specifically, a change to an upstream public model's contract or a cross-project ref() target might not trigger the downstream project's CI at all if each project's Slim CI only evaluates state within its own manifest, missing the cross-project blast radius entirely. The fix: verify and automate manifest freshness (pulling the actual latest production artifact as part of CI setup, with an explicit staleness check that fails loudly rather than silently using an old one), audit exactly what state:modified+ covers in the dbt version deployed and supplement with explicit test coverage on macros/sources that fall outside it, and for cross-project dependencies, add a deliberate cross-project impact check (or lean on dbt Mesh's own cross-project state comparison features where available) rather than assuming single-project Slim CI covers the whole dependency graph.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check, before assuming anything about dbt itself, is whether the manifest Slim CI is comparing against is actually current -- because state:modified+ is only as good as the baseline it's diffing against, and if that baseline is a few merges behind, it'll correctly miss changes that happened since then. That's turned out to be the cause more times than I'd like to admit. If the manifest is current, my next check is whether the breaking change was something state comparison even tracks by default -- a macro change, a source freshness definition, something in the Jinja context -- because not everything a developer would call 'a change' necessarily changes a model's own file in a way the comparison flags. And since this is a multi-project setup, I'd specifically check whether the change crossed a project boundary -- if it touched a public model's contract that a different project's CI never even looks at, that's a real gap in how Slim CI is scoped per-project, not a bug exactly, but a blind spot we need to close deliberately. My fix is threefold: make manifest freshness something CI actively verifies and fails on if it's stale, rather than something we assume; explicitly document and test the categories of change that fall outside default state comparison; and add a real cross-project impact check so a contract change in one project can't silently sail past the CI of every project depending on it.

Doesn't verify exactly what state:modified+ tracks in the dbt version in use (macros, sources, env context)
Misses that a cross-project contract change may not trigger downstream project CI in a Mesh setup
No automated staleness check on the production manifest used for comparison
Treats a passed Slim CI run as a complete correctness guarantee rather than a scoped one

Checks what state:modified+ actually tracks vs. assumes it covers everything
Identifies the cross-project Mesh blind spot for contract changes
Proposes an automated manifest-freshness check as a durable fix
Supplements Slim CI with explicit coverage for change types it doesn't catch

questions.title: A Sudden Snowflake Credit Spike on a Shared Multi-Cluster Warehouse
questions.prompt: A shared BI warehouse's credit consumption triples overnight with no known deployment or usage pattern change that anyone will admit to. Write the diagnostic queries you'd run against Snowflake's account usage views to find the actual cause, and walk through the likely culprits.
questions.code:
-- 1. Credit consumption by warehouse over time, to confirm scope and timing
SELECT warehouse_name, DATE_TRUNC('hour', start_time) AS hr, SUM(credits_used) AS credits
FROM snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_metering_history
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD('day', -3, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 2 DESC;

-- 2. Which queries/users actually drove the spike
SELECT user_name, query_type, warehouse_name,
       COUNT(*) AS query_count,
       SUM(execution_time)/1000 AS total_exec_sec,
       SUM(bytes_scanned)/POWER(1024,3) AS gb_scanned
FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history
WHERE warehouse_name = 'BI_SHARED_WH'
  AND start_time >= DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY total_exec_sec DESC
LIMIT 25;

-- 3. Cluster count over time, to detect a concurrency-driven multi-cluster scale-out
SELECT warehouse_name, start_time, avg_running, avg_queued_load
FROM snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_load_history
WHERE warehouse_name = 'BI_SHARED_WH'
  AND start_time >= DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY start_time;
questions.modelAnswer: The investigation has to separate two very different causes that both show up as 'credits tripled': a few genuinely heavy, expensive queries running on a normal cluster count, versus the multi-cluster warehouse scaling out to many more clusters than usual because of a concurrency spike -- the fix is completely different depending on which one it is, so I wouldn't act until I've confirmed which. The warehouse_metering_history query establishes scope and timing precisely (which warehouse, which hour), which matters because 'overnight' is vague and the real spike window might be much narrower. The query_history breakdown by user and query_type is where the actual culprit usually surfaces: at this scale, the most common causes are a new or modified scheduled job that regressed (a dbt model that lost a filter and now full-scans a huge table), a BI tool misconfigured to auto-refresh dashboards far more frequently than intended (minutes instead of hours), or a single analyst's ad hoc query doing an unintentionally expensive join/scan repeatedly in a loop or dashboard auto-refresh. The warehouse_load_history query tells you whether this was a concurrency event (many more clusters spun up to serve a burst of simultaneous queries) versus a small number of queries each individually consuming far more compute -- a spike in avg_running/avg_queued_load points to concurrency (new users, a misconfigured automated refresh hitting the warehouse constantly), while a spike concentrated in a handful of long-running, high-byte-scanned queries points to a regression in query efficiency, not demand. Once identified, the fix is specific to the cause -- rolling back or fixing the regressed job, correcting a dashboard refresh interval, or adding a resource monitor/warehouse-level guardrail -- not a blanket 'reduce warehouse size' response that might not even address what actually happened.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I jump to any conclusion about what caused this, I want three numbers: exactly when the spike started and on which warehouse, which specific queries or users actually drove the increase, and whether the warehouse was running more clusters than normal. That third one matters more than people expect -- tripled credits could mean a handful of queries got a lot more expensive, or it could mean the same queries as always just got hit by three times as many concurrent users or a dashboard that's refreshing way more often than it should. Those have completely different fixes. Pulling query_history grouped by user and query type almost always finds it -- the usual suspects I'm looking for are a scheduled job that regressed, like a dbt model that lost a filter and started full-scanning something huge, or a BI tool set to auto-refresh every few minutes instead of every few hours without anyone noticing. If instead the load history shows a bunch of extra clusters spinning up, that points at a concurrency story -- new users, or something hammering the warehouse repeatedly -- rather than any one query getting slower. I wouldn't recommend 'just shrink the warehouse' as a response until I know which of these it actually was, because that fix only works for one of the two possible causes and does nothing for the other.
commonMistakes: Recommends shrinking or reconfiguring the warehouse before diagnosing the actual cause
Doesn't distinguish a concurrency-driven multi-cluster scale-out from a small number of individually expensive queries
Skips checking for a misconfigured BI dashboard auto-refresh interval as a common real-world cause
Uses imprecise time windows instead of pinpointing the exact spike window first
Writes incorrect or non-functional ACCOUNT_USAGE queries
keyPoints: Pinpoints the exact spike window and warehouse before theorizing a cause
Distinguishes concurrency-driven scale-out from individually expensive query regressions
Checks for common real-world causes: regressed scheduled job, misconfigured dashboard refresh
Writes correct, working ACCOUNT_USAGE diagnostic SQL
Matches the fix to the diagnosed cause rather than a generic response

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working diagnostic SQL against ACCOUNT_USAGE views
Distinguishes concurrency-driven vs. query-efficiency causes
Identifies realistic, specific real-world culprits
Matches proposed fix to the diagnosed root cause

questions.title: Unity Catalog Permission Drift Silently Breaks Pipelines Across Workspaces
questions.prompt: Three independent teams' production pipelines, spread across different Databricks workspaces attached to the same Unity Catalog metastore, start failing with permission-denied errors on tables they've successfully read from for months. No one on the data platform team made a deliberate change. Diagnose the likely causes of this kind of cross-workspace permission drift, and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A multi-team, multi-workspace failure like this that 'nobody deliberately changed' almost always traces to a change made for a legitimate, narrow reason that had a broader blast radius than whoever made it realized, because Unity Catalog's grants are metastore-scoped and apply consistently across every workspace attached to it -- a change made while thinking only about one workspace's needs can break three others instantly. The most common specific causes: a group membership change (someone removed from or restructured within an Entra ID/Okta group that a grant was scoped to, rather than to an individual user, so a routine HR/identity-system sync silently revoked access for everyone in that group); a grant that was applied with an expiration or as part of a time-boxed access request that quietly lapsed; or a catalog/schema-level grant being revoked or narrowed as part of an unrelated security hardening pass that didn't account for who else depended on that broader grant. The fix starts with the audit log: Unity Catalog's access events are logged, so I'd query system tables (or the account's audit log export) for GRANT/REVOKE events on the affected objects in the time window before the failures started, which should name exactly what changed and who/what made the change, turning 'nobody did anything' into a concrete answer almost every time. The durable fix is process, not just restoring the grant: require that any grant or group-membership change touching an object used by multiple teams' production pipelines go through a lightweight review that's actually aware of who depends on that object -- which is only possible if dependency/consumer information is tracked somewhere (even a simple registry of 'which pipelines read this table'), because without that, the person making a seemingly-local change has no way to know the blast radius they're about to create.
questions.professionalAnswer: When three unrelated teams break at once with no deliberate change from the platform team, my instinct is that someone made a change for a reason that made sense in isolation, and the blast radius was bigger than they realized -- because grants in Unity Catalog aren't scoped to a workspace, they're scoped to the metastore, so a change made thinking about one workspace's problem can quietly take down three others that happen to share the same underlying object. I'd go straight to the audit trail rather than guessing -- Unity Catalog logs grant and revoke events, so pulling that history for the affected tables in the window before things broke almost always gives you a precise answer: a group's membership got restructured by an identity-system sync, a time-boxed access grant quietly expired, or a security hardening pass narrowed a catalog-level grant without realizing three production pipelines were relying on it. Fixing the immediate grant gets everyone back online, but the real fix is making sure whoever makes a change like that next time actually knows who depends on the thing they're about to touch -- which means we need some kind of registry of which pipelines consume which tables, even a simple one, because right now that knowledge lives only in people's heads, and that's exactly how 'nobody changed anything' incidents like this keep happening.
commonMistakes: Assumes the grant change itself was the whole story without investigating group-membership or expiration causes
Doesn't use Unity Catalog's audit log/system tables to find the actual grant/revoke event
Restores the broken grant without addressing the process gap that allowed an unreviewed, cross-team-impacting change
Assumes grants are workspace-scoped rather than correctly understanding they're metastore-scoped
No dependency tracking to know which teams/pipelines rely on a given shared object
keyPoints: Correctly identifies metastore-scoped grants as the reason a 'local' change had cross-workspace impact
Considers group-membership changes and expiring time-boxed grants as common root causes
Uses Unity Catalog's audit log/system tables to find the actual causal event
Fixes the immediate grant issue while addressing the underlying process gap
Proposes dependency/consumer tracking to prevent recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about metastore-scoped grants causing cross-workspace impact
Identifies realistic, specific root causes (group membership, expiring grants)
Proposes using the audit log to find the actual causal event
Proposes a durable process fix (dependency tracking/review), not just restoring access

questions.title: Terraform State Lock Contention and Drift Across 15 Teams
questions.prompt: Multiple teams sharing a Terraform setup report increasingly frequent 'state lock' errors blocking their applies, and separately, a growing number of resources show drift (the real cloud resource no longer matches what's in state) that nobody can explain. Diagnose both problems and the fixes, including whether they're actually related.
questions.modelAnswer: These two symptoms are related, but not in the way they might first appear: they're both downstream consequences of too many independent actors sharing too little isolation, rather than one causing the other directly. Lock contention happens when multiple applies attempt to run against the same state file concurrently -- if 15 teams share fewer state files than teams (a common anti-pattern as a platform scales faster than its state-isolation design), then normal, unrelated work from different teams collides on the same lock, and the fix is structural: split shared state into per-team, per-environment state files so unrelated teams' applies simply can't contend for the same lock, rather than trying to coordinate human scheduling around applies, which never holds up as team count grows. Drift, separately, usually comes from one of three sources at this scale: manual out-of-band changes made directly in the cloud console (someone 'just quickly' fixing something without going through Terraform, which is almost always a process/culture gap, not a tooling one), a resource being managed by more than one Terraform configuration or by Terraform and a separate automation tool simultaneously, or a stuck/abandoned lock from a previous failed apply that got force-unlocked incorrectly, leaving state and reality out of sync from that point forward. I'd diagnose drift concretely with terraform plan run regularly (ideally on a schedule, not just before someone's next deliberate change) to surface every drifted resource with a diff, rather than waiting for someone to stumble onto a mismatch; the plan output itself usually makes the cause obvious (a tag or setting that doesn't match any recent Terraform change points to manual console edits). The durable fix for both: split state per team/environment to eliminate most lock contention structurally, enforce that all infrastructure changes go through Terraform via policy and access restrictions (removing direct console write access for resources under Terraform management where feasible), and run scheduled drift-detection plans with alerting so drift surfaces within hours, not whenever someone happens to notice.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd actually separate these into two problems first, because treating them as one thing will send the investigation in the wrong direction. The lock contention is almost certainly a structural problem: if 15 teams are sharing state files that don't map one-to-one with teams and environments, unrelated applies are going to collide on the same lock constantly, and no amount of 'please coordinate in Slack before you apply' is going to hold up as the team count grows -- the actual fix is splitting state per team per environment so there's nothing left to contend over. Drift is a separate story, and in my experience it's almost always one of three things: someone made a quick manual fix directly in the cloud console because it felt faster than going through a PR, a resource is quietly being managed by two different things at once, or a previous apply got stuck, someone force-unlocked it without really checking what state it left things in, and drift crept in from that point forward. I wouldn't wait for someone to stumble onto a mismatch -- I'd set up a scheduled terraform plan that runs regularly just to surface drift as a diff, so we catch it within hours instead of discovering it during an incident. And for the console-edit case specifically, the real fix isn't technical, it's tightening who has direct write access to resources that are supposed to be managed entirely through Terraform.

Proposes human coordination/scheduling to fix lock contention instead of structural state isolation
Doesn't consider manual console edits as a likely drift cause
No scheduled, proactive drift-detection process, relying on accidental discovery
Force-unlocks stuck state without investigating whether it left state inconsistent with reality
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes lock contention from drift as related but separate problems
Proposes structural state isolation (per team/environment) rather than coordination as the lock-contention fix
Identifies realistic drift causes: manual console edits, dual management, mishandled force-unlocks
Proposes scheduled, proactive drift detection rather than reactive discovery
Proposes restricting direct console access as part of the durable fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses and distinguishes both problems
Proposes structural state isolation as the lock-contention fix
Identifies realistic, specific drift causes
Proposes proactive, scheduled drift detection and access controls

questions.title: Fabric Capacity Throttling Takes Down Everyone's Reports at Once
questions.prompt: A Fabric capacity shared across 8 business units starts throttling in the afternoon every day, and when it throttles, every workspace on that capacity -- including ones doing nothing heavy -- sees report refresh failures and slow interactive queries. Diagnose why throttling affects even idle workspaces, and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Fabric capacity throttling isn't scoped per-workspace, it's scoped to the whole capacity: when the capacity's consumed compute exceeds what its smoothing/bursting model can absorb, Fabric starts rejecting or delaying interactive operations across every workspace assigned to that capacity, including ones that aren't doing anything heavy themselves -- an idle workspace isn't protected from a noisy neighbor just because it isn't the cause, because the throttle is a property of the shared capacity resource, not of any individual workspace's own usage. The daily afternoon pattern is the useful diagnostic clue: it points to a predictable, recurring workload rather than a random spike -- most commonly a scheduled refresh (a semantic model or dataflow refresh scheduled for early afternoon across several business units simultaneously) or an interactive-usage peak that happens to coincide with when most of the 8 business units' analysts are actively working. I'd confirm this with the Fabric Capacity Metrics app, looking at per-workspace and per-operation CU consumption specifically in the afternoon window, to identify which specific workload (which refresh, which workspace) is actually driving the capacity over its throttling threshold. The fix follows directly from that diagnosis: if it's a clustering of scheduled refreshes, stagger them across the day so they don't all compete for capacity at the same hour; if it's organic interactive-usage overlap across 8 business units that's simply outgrown the capacity's real throughput, that's a genuine capacity-sizing or segmentation conversation (separating heavier business units onto their own capacity), not something staggered scheduling alone fixes. Either way, the fix is never 'just upsize blindly' before the metrics identify which of those two very different problems is actually happening.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part that's confusing people is why an idle workspace gets hit by throttling too, and the answer is that throttling isn't a per-workspace thing in Fabric -- it's a property of the whole capacity. If the capacity as a whole is over its threshold, it doesn't matter that your workspace didn't do anything; everyone on that shared resource feels it together. The fact that it happens every afternoon, at roughly the same time, tells me this isn't random noise -- that's the signature of a recurring, scheduled workload, most likely several business units' refreshes landing in the same window, or just everyone's interactive usage peaking at the same time of day. I'd pull up the Capacity Metrics app and look specifically at that afternoon window, per workspace and per operation, to find exactly what's driving it over the line, rather than guessing. If it turns out to be a pile of scheduled refreshes all firing around the same hour, the fix is just staggering them across the day -- cheap and immediate. If it's genuinely organic usage across 8 business units that's simply outgrown what this capacity can handle, that's a different conversation about either a bigger SKU or splitting the heaviest business units onto their own capacity -- but I want the metrics to tell me which of those two it actually is before I spend money on either one.
commonMistakes: Assumes throttling only affects the workspace causing the heavy load
Doesn't recognize capacity throttling as a shared-resource property affecting every attached workspace
Jumps to upsizing the capacity before diagnosing what's actually driving the afternoon spike
Doesn't use the daily recurring pattern as a diagnostic clue pointing to scheduled workloads
Proposes staggering refreshes as a fix for what's actually organic usage growth, or vice versa
keyPoints: Correctly explains throttling as a capacity-wide property affecting all attached workspaces
Uses the recurring daily pattern as a diagnostic clue pointing to scheduled or peak-usage causes
Uses the Capacity Metrics app to pinpoint the actual driving workload
Distinguishes a staggering fix (scheduled refresh clustering) from a sizing/segmentation fix (organic growth)
Avoids upsizing blindly before the metrics identify the real cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains capacity-wide throttling affecting all workspaces
Proposes a concrete diagnostic approach using real metrics
Distinguishes between the two realistic root causes and their distinct fixes
Avoids a premature, unverified fix

questions.title: A Platform Migration Cutover Fails Halfway Through
questions.prompt: You're migrating a legacy data warehouse to a new lakehouse platform. Mid-cutover -- half the downstream BI reports repointed to the new platform, half still on the old one -- a critical data quality issue is discovered in the new platform's output. Walk through how you'd triage and stabilize in the moment, and the structural mistake in the migration plan that likely allowed this situation to happen at all.
questions.modelAnswer: In the moment, the first priority is containment, not root-cause analysis: stop any further reports from being repointed to the new platform until the data quality issue is understood, and assess whether the reports already repointed are serving genuinely wrong numbers right now -- if so, that's a live data-correctness incident requiring immediate communication to whoever consumes those specific reports, not a quiet background fix. I'd establish a fast, clear answer to 'which reports are on which platform right now' (this should already exist as a migration tracking artifact, not something assembled under pressure during the incident) so the blast radius is known precisely rather than guessed at. Given the structural problem exists, I would not attempt to simply roll everything back to the old platform as a blanket reflex -- if the old platform's pipeline has already been decommissioned or its data has drifted since cutover began, rollback might not actually be safe or even possible for every repointed report, so each affected report needs its specific rollback feasibility assessed, not assumed. The structural mistake that allowed this: a migration plan that didn't define or enforce the cutover as reversible in small, independently verifiable batches with a validation gate at each batch -- if reports were repointed in large batches, or without diffing new-platform output against old-platform output on real data before repointing each one, then a data quality defect that should have been caught before any report moved was instead discovered only after a meaningful fraction of production reporting was already dependent on the new platform. The fix going forward: pause the cutover, revert the specific affected reports where safe, fix and re-validate the data quality issue against a diff harness comparing both platforms' output, and resume cutover in smaller batches with a mandatory pre-cutover validation gate per batch rather than per-report ad hoc judgment calls.
questions.professionalAnswer: In the moment, my first job is containment, not figuring out why this happened -- I want to stop any more reports getting repointed right now, and I want a precise, immediate answer to which specific reports are already on the new platform, because that's my actual blast radius. If any of those are serving wrong numbers to someone right now, that's a live incident and the people relying on those specific reports need to hear it from us before they find it themselves. I wouldn't reflexively roll everything back to the old platform either -- if that pipeline's already been partially decommissioned or its data's drifted since the cutover started, rollback might genuinely not be safe for every report, so I'd check that per report rather than assume it. Once things are stable, the harder conversation is what let this happen at all, and honestly, the answer is usually that the migration moved in batches too large, without a real validation gate comparing new-platform output against old-platform output on actual data before each batch got repointed. If that comparison had been mandatory per batch, this data quality issue should have been caught before a single report moved, not after half of them already had. Going forward, I'd pause, fix the issue, re-validate with an actual diff harness, and resume in smaller batches with that validation gate as a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Assumes a blanket rollback to the old platform is always safe without checking per-report feasibility
Has no existing tracking artifact for which reports are on which platform during the migration
Doesn't identify large, unvalidated cutover batches as the structural root cause
No plan to re-validate with a diff harness before resuming cutover
keyPoints: Prioritizes containment and precise blast-radius assessment over root-cause analysis in the moment
Assesses rollback feasibility per report rather than assuming a blanket rollback is safe
Identifies large, unvalidated batch cutover as the structural root cause
Proposes resuming with a mandatory per-batch validation/diff gate
Treats migration tracking as something that should already exist, not be improvised mid-incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct in-the-moment triage and containment approach
Correctly avoids assuming blanket rollback is safe
Identifies the structural root cause (batch size/validation gate)
Proposes a durable fix for resuming the migration safely

questions.title: A Silent Data Contract Violation Corrupts Twelve Downstream Consumers
questions.prompt: A producing team changed the meaning (not the type or name) of a field -- a 'status' field that used to mean order status now means fulfillment status after a business logic change -- without any schema change for a data contract to catch. Twelve downstream consumers silently computed wrong aggregates for weeks before anyone noticed. Diagnose why your contract enforcement didn't catch this, and what you'd add to catch this class of issue in the future.
questions.modelAnswer: Schema-based data contracts (JSON Schema, Avro, a type/column definition) enforce structure -- field names, types, nullability -- but they have no mechanism to express or verify semantic meaning, so a change that preserves the exact same field name and type while silently changing what that field represents is, by design, invisible to a purely structural contract; this isn't a bug in the contract enforcement, it's a category of change the enforcement was never built to catch. The reason it went undetected for weeks rather than immediately is that the downstream consumers' aggregates didn't produce obviously wrong-looking output (a status field still contained valid-looking enum values, just now meaning something different), so nothing failed loudly -- it degraded silently into wrong numbers that looked plausible. To catch this class of issue, structural contracts alone aren't enough; I'd add: a semantic field description as a required, versioned part of every contract (not just name/type, but what the field actually represents, enforced as documentation that has to change -- and thus be reviewed -- whenever the meaning changes, even if the type doesn't), paired with a lightweight but mandatory change-review process requiring the producing team to flag any semantic/business-logic change to a field, not just structural ones, since that's a social/process gap a schema can't close alone. Technically, I'd add statistical drift monitoring on key fields' value distributions (if 'status' suddenly has a materially different distribution of values across its enum, or its correlation with other fields shifts sharply, that's a signal worth alerting on even though no schema validation failed) and require downstream consumers of contracted fields to register which fields they actually depend on semantically, so a producing team can be shown 'these 12 consumers depend on this field's current meaning' before making a change, rather than the dependency being invisible until something breaks.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer here is that our contract did exactly what it was designed to do, and that's the problem -- it checks structure, not meaning, and this change didn't touch structure at all. The field kept the same name, same type, same valid values; it just started meaning something different, and there's no way a schema validator catches that, because that's not a question a schema can even ask. It went unnoticed for weeks specifically because nothing looked wrong -- the numbers were just quietly, plausibly wrong, which is a lot scarier than a loud failure. So the fix isn't 'make the contract stricter,' it's recognizing we need a second layer that isn't purely structural. I'd make every contracted field carry a real semantic description as part of its versioned definition, not just a type, and require that any change to what a field means -- even with no type change -- go through the same review process as a breaking schema change, because functionally, to the twelve teams depending on it, it was one. I'd also want statistical monitoring on key fields' value distributions, because a sudden shift in how a field's values are distributed is exactly the kind of signal that would have caught this in days instead of weeks, even though no schema check would ever fire on it. And longer term, I want downstream teams to register which fields they actually depend on semantically, so the next time someone on the producing team wants to change what a field means, they can see exactly who that's going to affect before they ship it, not after.

Doesn't recognize that semantic meaning changes are structurally invisible to type/name-based contracts
Proposes only stricter schema validation, which cannot address this class of issue at all
No statistical/distributional monitoring to catch silent semantic drift
No mechanism for downstream teams to register semantic dependencies on specific fields

Explains why this failure mode is silent rather than loud
Proposes versioned semantic field descriptions with mandatory review on meaning changes
Proposes statistical drift monitoring on field value distributions as a technical backstop
Proposes downstream semantic-dependency registration to make blast radius visible before a change ships

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the structural-vs-semantic contract gap
Explains why the failure was silent rather than immediately detected
Proposes a sound semantic-contract/review mechanism
Proposes a technical monitoring backstop (distributional drift)

questions.title: Build vs. Buy for a Whole Data Platform's Orchestration Layer
questions.prompt: A newly-acquired business unit's leadership wants to build a custom, in-house orchestration framework rather than adopt your platform's existing Airflow standard, arguing their pipeline needs are 'too unique.' As the principal responsible for platform consistency, walk through the build-vs-buy framework you'd actually apply, and how you'd evaluate whether their needs are genuinely unique or just unfamiliar with the existing tool.
questions.modelAnswer: A sound build-vs-buy framework for platform-level decisions weighs four things, not just feature fit: whether the genuine requirement gap is real and large enough to justify a parallel system (most 'we're unique' claims collapse once you separate the business unit's actual orchestration requirements from their team's unfamiliarity with the existing tool); the total cost of ownership of building and maintaining a second orchestration system indefinitely, including on-call burden, security patching, and the hidden tax of every other team now needing to understand two systems instead of one; the opportunity cost of the engineering time spent building versus adopting; and the organizational cost of platform fragmentation itself -- every additional bespoke system makes cross-team observability, incident response, and hiring (new engineers now need two skill sets) measurably harder, which is a real cost even when nobody budgets for it explicitly. My evaluation process: have the business unit document their specific technical requirements that they believe Airflow can't meet, then have a platform engineer who knows Airflow deeply (not the requesting team, who has an incentive to find gaps) assess each one against the existing platform's actual capabilities and extension points (custom operators, plugins, sensors) -- in my experience, the overwhelming majority of 'too unique' claims turn out to be solvable with a custom operator or a different pattern within the existing tool, not a genuine platform gap. If a genuine, well-documented gap remains after that honest assessment, I'd evaluate extending the existing platform first, and only approve a separate system as a last resort with an explicit sunset/consolidation plan, never as an open-ended parallel standard.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't say no immediately, but I also wouldn't take 'our needs are too unique' at face value, because that's the single most common thing I hear right before a team builds something expensive that turns out to have a one-line fix in the tool they already have. My first ask is concrete: write down the specific things you believe Airflow can't do for you. Then I'd have someone who actually knows our Airflow setup deeply -- not the team asking for the exception, because they're not a neutral party here -- go through that list and check it against what the platform can already do, including custom operators and plugins, not just the out-of-the-box feature set. Nine times out of ten in my experience, what looked like a fundamental gap turns out to be unfamiliarity with an existing extension point. If something genuinely doesn't fit after that honest look, my next move is extending the platform, not standing up a second one -- because a second orchestration system isn't just their cost, it's a tax on every other team's on-call rotation, hiring requirements, and incident response from here on out. I'd only approve a fully separate system as a last resort, and even then, with a clear, time-bound plan for either consolidating it back in or formally supporting it long-term, not an indefinite exception nobody revisits.

Doesn't weigh the organizational cost of platform fragmentation (on-call, hiring, observability)
Has the requesting team assess their own requirement gap instead of a neutral platform expert
Treats build and buy as a one-time decision with no sunset/consolidation plan for an approved exception
Dismisses the request outright without a genuine evaluation process

Requires a neutral, platform-expert assessment of the claimed requirement gap

questions.title: System Design: Choosing a Platform Strategy for a 25-Team Data Org
questions.prompt: A 500-person company with 25 data-consuming teams is consolidating onto a single lakehouse/warehouse strategy after years of ad hoc tool choices. Current state: heavy Python/ML workloads on a few teams, heavy BI/reporting on most teams, strong existing Power BI investment, moderate but real cost sensitivity, and a 9-month deadline. Decide between Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric, and a multi-platform strategy, and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: With a strong existing Power BI investment, a 9-month deadline, and most of the 25 teams doing BI/reporting rather than heavy ML, Microsoft Fabric is the strongest default candidate: Direct Lake mode gives near-instant Power BI performance against OneLake without a separate semantic-layer rebuild, the unified SaaS experience lowers the operational burden a 9-month timeline can't absorb if it required building a platform team from scratch, and licensing is often more cost-predictable for an org already paying for Power BI/Microsoft 365 than a net-new platform vendor relationship. The real risk is the handful of heavy Python/ML teams: Fabric's Spark/notebook experience is real but materially less mature for complex ML workflows than Databricks', so forcing those specific teams onto Fabric purely for platform uniformity risks their productivity and could become the reason the whole migration gets blamed later. My recommendation is a deliberately narrow multi-platform strategy, not a free-for-all: Fabric as the default platform for the 20+ BI-centric teams, with the handful of genuinely ML-heavy teams staying on or moving to Databricks for their workloads specifically, connected via OneLake's ability to shortcut/reference Delta tables so data doesn't have to be duplicated across platforms. I would not recommend Snowflake here primarily because it doesn't leverage the existing Power BI investment as directly as Fabric's Direct Lake does, and introducing a third major vendor relationship when two platforms already cover the real workload split adds unnecessary cost and operational surface for this specific org's constraints. The governance guardrail that makes this safe rather than a slippery slope back to ad hoc tool sprawl: a documented, narrow criterion for which teams qualify for the Databricks exception (demonstrated, sustained heavy ML/Spark workload, not just a preference), reviewed periodically, not an open door.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given what's described -- heavy Power BI investment already in place, most of the 25 teams doing BI and reporting rather than ML, and a 9-month clock -- I'd lead with Fabric as the default, because Direct Lake mode against OneLake plugs straight into the Power BI investment this company has already made, and a unified SaaS platform is just a much more realistic operational lift to stand up in 9 months than building out a full platform team around a different vendor. Where I'd push back on a pure one-platform answer is the ML-heavy teams -- Databricks' notebook and Spark experience for serious ML work is genuinely more mature right now, and if I force those specific teams onto Fabric just for uniformity's sake, I'm trading their productivity for a cleanliness that doesn't actually serve the business. So my real recommendation is a narrow two-platform strategy: Fabric for the 20-plus BI-centric teams, Databricks for the small number of teams doing real, sustained ML work, connected through OneLake shortcuts so we're not duplicating data between them. I'd explicitly leave Snowflake out of this one, because it doesn't buy us anything the existing Power BI investment doesn't already get us more directly through Fabric, and three platforms is one more than this specific workload split justifies. The guardrail I'd insist on: a real, documented bar for which teams get the Databricks exception, reviewed on a schedule, so this doesn't quietly turn back into the tool sprawl we're trying to consolidate out of.
commonMistakes: Picks one platform dogmatically without weighing the existing Power BI investment or the ML-heavy teams' needs
Recommends Snowflake without explaining what it adds given the stated Power BI/BI-heavy context
Proposes an unlimited multi-platform strategy with no governance boundary, recreating the original tool sprawl
Ignores the 9-month deadline's real constraint on operational buildout complexity
Doesn't address data duplication/integration between the two platforms chosen
keyPoints: Weighs the existing Power BI investment and Direct Lake's fit for most teams
Recognizes Databricks' relative ML/Spark maturity advantage for the ML-heavy minority
Proposes a deliberately narrow, governed multi-platform strategy rather than one-size-fits-all or unlimited sprawl
Explains why Snowflake is not the best fit given this org's specific constraints
Addresses integration (OneLake shortcuts) to avoid data duplication across the two platforms

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Makes and justifies a platform recommendation fitting the stated constraints
Correctly weighs the ML-heavy minority's needs against platform uniformity
Proposes a governed, bounded multi-platform approach rather than unlimited sprawl
Addresses integration/data-duplication between chosen platforms

deepDive.heading: Clarify requirements and constraints
deepDive.content: The decisive constraints are: a 9-month deadline (rules out anything requiring a large net-new platform team), a strong existing Power BI investment (a sunk cost that strongly favors whichever platform integrates most directly with it), a minority of teams with genuinely heavy ML/Spark needs (a real technical requirement, not a preference), and moderate cost sensitivity (argues against paying for three major platforms when two cover the real workload split).

deepDive.heading: Default platform for the BI-centric majority
deepDive.content: Fabric's Direct Lake mode queries Delta tables in OneLake directly without a separate import/aggregation step, giving Power BI reports near-real-time performance against the lake with no semantic-model rebuild — this directly leverages the existing Power BI investment rather than requiring 20+ teams to relearn a new BI stack on top of a new data platform simultaneously.

deepDive.heading: The ML-heavy minority
deepDive.content: Databricks' notebook-first, Spark-native workflow and MLflow integration remain materially more mature for complex feature engineering, model training, and experiment tracking than Fabric's current Spark/notebook experience. Forcing these teams onto Fabric purely for platform uniformity trades their productivity for a cleanliness the business doesn't actually need, and risks those specific teams becoming the migration's most visible failure story.

deepDive.heading: Integration without duplication
deepDive.content: OneLake's shortcut capability lets Fabric reference Delta tables that physically live in Databricks-managed storage (and vice versa) without copying data, so the two platforms can share a single physical copy of shared datasets rather than each team's workload requiring its own duplicated ETL into its preferred platform.

deepDive.heading: Governance guardrail against renewed sprawl
deepDive.content: A narrow, documented, periodically-reviewed criterion for which teams qualify for the Databricks exception (demonstrated sustained ML/Spark workload, not preference) is what keeps this a deliberate two-platform strategy rather than a slide back into the ad hoc tool sprawl the consolidation was meant to fix.

deepDive.heading: What I'd watch post-rollout
deepDive.content: Track whether any BI-centric team on Fabric starts requesting ML capability (a sign the boundary needs revisiting) and whether Databricks team count creeps upward without a corresponding documented workload justification (a sign the exception process is being gamed).

questions.title: Streaming vs. Batch at Petabyte Scale: Where the Economics Actually Flip
questions.prompt: A platform processing several petabytes a month of clickstream and IoT data runs almost entirely batch today, on a daily cadence, and leadership wants to know whether moving to streaming is worth it. Walk through the real economics and operational tradeoffs of streaming vs. batch at this scale, and how you'd decide where it's actually worth the investment versus where daily batch remains correct.
questions.modelAnswer: At petabyte scale, the batch-vs-streaming decision is not a technology preference, it's an economics question with a specific break-even point: streaming infrastructure (always-on Kafka brokers, always-on stream processors) has a continuous baseline compute and operational cost that batch doesn't, since batch only pays for compute during its scheduled run window, so streaming is only worth it when the business value of lower latency genuinely exceeds that continuous cost -- and 'genuinely exceeds' needs to be demonstrated with a real latency-to-value argument, not assumed. The honest framework: identify which specific use cases actually need sub-hour (or sub-minute) freshness and can show a concrete business consequence of not having it (fraud detection, real-time personalization, operational alerting), versus which use cases are consumed by humans who check a dashboard once a day or less and genuinely don't benefit from fresher data no matter how fast the pipeline runs underneath them -- the latter should stay batch regardless of what's technically possible, because streaming them would add real operational cost and complexity (schema evolution handling, exactly-once concerns, 24/7 on-call for infrastructure that never sleeps) for zero realized business value. At this scale, I'd also flag that a full move to streaming doesn't remove the need for a batch-equivalent capability: a durable, replayable raw layer and the ability to recompute history correctly after a logic bug or business rule change remains necessary regardless of whether the live path is streaming, which is exactly the Lambda-architecture tradeoff -- streaming doesn't make that need go away, it just changes where the 'batch-equivalent' recompute capability lives. My recommendation to leadership: audit use cases by actual latency sensitivity and business impact, move only the handful that clear that bar to streaming, and explicitly keep the rest on batch, framing this as a deliberate cost-benefit decision per use case rather than a platform-wide migration.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'should we move to streaming' as a single yes/no question, because at this volume it's really 25 or 30 smaller questions, one per real use case, and most of them probably have the same answer: no, not worth it. Streaming infrastructure is running all the time, which means it's costing money and needing on-call attention all the time, where batch only costs you during its run window. That's fine to pay for when the business genuinely needs the freshness -- fraud detection catching something in seconds instead of a day later is a real, demonstrable difference. It's not fine to pay for just so a dashboard someone checks once a day looks marginally more real-time, because nobody's actually making a different decision because of those extra hours of freshness. So my actual recommendation is an audit: go through the real use cases, find the ones with a genuine, demonstrable latency-to-business-value argument, and move just those to streaming. Everything else stays on batch, on purpose, not because we didn't get around to it. And I'd flag one more thing leadership might not expect: even for what does move to streaming, we still need a durable, replayable raw layer underneath it, because the ability to recompute history correctly when logic changes doesn't go away just because the live path got faster -- streaming changes where that capability lives, it doesn't eliminate the need for it.
commonMistakes: Treats streaming as a universal upgrade over batch without a real cost-benefit framework
Doesn't identify which specific use cases have a demonstrable latency-to-business-value argument
Ignores the continuous operational cost (on-call, infrastructure uptime) of streaming vs. batch's bounded run-window cost
Assumes moving to streaming eliminates the need for a durable, replayable recompute capability
Proposes an all-or-nothing platform migration instead of a per-use-case decision
keyPoints: Frames the decision as an economics question with a real break-even point, not a technology preference
Requires a demonstrable latency-to-business-value argument per use case before recommending streaming
Identifies continuous operational cost as streaming's real tradeoff against batch
Recognizes that a durable, replayable raw layer remains necessary even for streaming use cases
Recommends a per-use-case decision rather than a platform-wide migration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the decision as economics/latency-value tradeoff, not technology preference
Proposes a concrete per-use-case evaluation framework
Accurately weighs streaming's continuous operational cost
Recognizes the continued need for durable, replayable raw data

questions.title: System Design: Multi-Region Disaster Recovery for a Regulated Data Platform
questions.prompt: Design a multi-region disaster recovery architecture for a data platform serving a financial services company, with a regulatory requirement of RPO under 15 minutes and RTO under 1 hour for core transactional and reporting data, operating across two cloud regions with data residency constraints preventing certain customer data from leaving its origin region.
questions.modelAnswer: RPO under 15 minutes rules out daily or even hourly batch-based backup as the DR mechanism for core data -- it requires continuous or near-continuous replication, so I'd use the storage/database layer's native cross-region replication (e.g., geo-redundant storage with change-feed-based replication, or a managed database's cross-region read replica with asynchronous replication tuned for sub-15-minute lag) rather than scheduled snapshot-and-copy jobs. RTO under 1 hour requires the secondary region to be warm, not cold -- infrastructure, access grants, and network configuration must already exist and be kept in sync (via the same IaC templates deployed to both regions, not manually recreated during an incident), because provisioning infrastructure from scratch during an actual disaster cannot realistically complete within an hour at this complexity. The data residency constraint is the most architecturally interesting piece: it means this cannot be a uniform 'replicate everything to the other region' design -- data subject to residency restrictions needs an in-region-only DR strategy (a second availability zone or a second facility within the same region, meeting RPO/RTO without crossing the border) while unrestricted data replicates cross-region normally, which means the platform needs a data classification tag that drives routing/replication decisions automatically rather than relying on engineers remembering which datasets are restricted. Failover itself must be driven by an automated, lag-aware process: health checks and replication-lag monitoring trigger (or recommend) failover, with the decision gated on confirming current replication lag is within the RPO bound at the moment of failover, so promoting a secondary that's actually lagging beyond the regulatory RPO doesn't quietly violate the very requirement the design was built to satisfy.
